items.stem: Operating at η = 0.92 (92%) efficiency from a 200 V rms AC source, a laminated-core hospital X-ray filament supply transformer has N_p = 1200 turns, N_s = 2400 turns, and a 6 Ω secondary load resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Applies turns-ratio equation V_s = V_p(N_s/N_p).
Obtains 400 V.
Uses P_out = V_s² / R_L.
Obtains 2.67 × 10⁴ W.
Uses P_in = P_out / η and I_p = P_in / V_p.
Obtains 145 A.

parts.prompt: Calculate the rms voltage across the secondary winding.
Determine the useful electrical power delivered to the secondary load.
Calculate the rms current drawn from the primary supply.

items.stem: Connected via slip rings to a 50 Ω load in a marine diesel-electric AC load-testing unit, an ideal coil of 100 turns and area 0.012 m² rotates at 80 Hz in a uniform 0.48 T magnetic field. What is the root-mean-square (rms) potential difference across the load?
items.workedSolution: Peak emf ε₀ = 2πfNBA = 2π(80)(100)(0.48)(0.012) = 290 V. Therefore V_rms = ε₀ / √2 = 205 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ε₀ = 2πfNBA and divides by √2 to obtain 205 V (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides peak emf ε₀ by 2 (confusing the ½ power factor with the 1/√2 rms voltage factor).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Stops at peak emf ε₀ = 2πfNBA without dividing by √2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies peak emf ε₀ by √2 instead of dividing by √2.

items.stem: Within a paleoclimate ice-core Bainbridge analyser, crossed selector fields E = 9.60 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B₁ = 0.35 T admit potassium isotopes of charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and masses m₁ = 6.47 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and m₂ = 6.81 × 10⁻²⁶ kg through slit S into a uniform B₂ = 0.7 T magnetic sector (out of the page).

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = E / B₁.
Obtains 2.74 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
Uses r₁ = m₁v / (qB₂) with chamber field B₂.
Obtains 0.158 m.
Doubles the radius difference ΔD = 2(r₂ − r₁).
Obtains 0.0167 m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the common speed of the ions emerging from the velocity selector.
Determine the orbital radius r₁ of the lighter isotope in the deflection chamber.
Calculate the separation ΔD between the two isotope strike points on the detector wall.

items.stem: In Required Practical 10, a stiff copper wire of active length $L = 50$ mm sits perpendicularly between slab magnets mounted on a steel yoke atop a 0.01 g digital top-pan balance ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). Plotting balance reading against current $I$ up to 4.0 A produces a straight line of gradient 0.367 g A⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $B = 72.0 mT$. (b) $F = 0.0144 N$. (c) $\Delta m = 1.47 g$. (d) by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current.

markScheme.criterion: Converts gradient to kg A⁻¹ and substitutes into $B = (\mathrm{grad}\cdot g)/L$.
Flux density $B = 72.0 mT$.
Substitutes into $F = B I L$.
Magnetic force $F = 0.0144 N$.
Converts $F/g$ into grams.
Mass change $\Delta m = 1.47 g$.
States magnetic field exerts an upward force on the clamped wire.
Applies Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite downward force on magnet yoke raises balance reading.

parts.prompt: Use the gradient to calculate the magnetic flux density $B$ in mT.
Calculate the magnetic force on the wire at the maximum current of 4.0 A.
Calculate the change in balance reading $\Delta m$ (in g) at this maximum current.
Explain using Newton's third law why the balance reading changes even though the wire is clamped independently.
parts.expectedAnswer: by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current
workingSteps: Magnetic field exerts an upward force BIl on the current-carrying wire.
By Newton's 3rd law, the wire exerts an equal downward force BIl on the magnets/yoke, increasing the balance normal reaction.

items.stem: In a magnetic calibration run, the axial flux density perpendicular to an electromagnet pole-gap calibration search coil with 350 turns, cross-section 0.01 m², and resistance 12 Ω switches from +0.12 T to −0.0720 T during an interval of 0.08 s. What is the magnitude of the average emf induced in the coil during the reversal?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates |ΔB| across sign reversal to obtain |ε| = 8.40 V (C).

options.distractorRationale: Treats the field as dropping only to zero (ΔB = B₁) rather than reversing sign to B₂.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the field magnitudes |B₁| − |B₂| instead of taking the signed vector difference |B₂ − B₁|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides emf by resistance R, reporting induced current instead of induced emf.

items.stem: Travelling to the left at constant velocity 8 m s⁻¹, a crossbar of resistance 1.2 Ω spans frictionless rails 0.2 m apart on a magnetohydrodynamic copper-bar carriage connected to a 1.4 Ω load in a 0.6 T field (directed out of the page). What is the terminal potential difference across the external load resistor?
items.workedSolution: ε = BLv = 0.960 V; loop current I = ε / (R + r) = 0.369 A. Terminal p.d. across load V_term = I R = 0.369 × 1.4 = 0.517 V.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_term = BLv × R/(R + r) to obtain 0.517 V (A).

items.stem: In the camera strobe decay module shown, a capacitor of capacitance C = 300 μF is first fully charged to V₀ = 10.0 V by closing Switch A while Switches B and C remain open. Switch A is then opened and Switch B is closed so the capacitor discharges through R₁ = 60 kΩ for 12.0 s. At t = 12.0 s, while Switch B stays closed, Switch C is closed to connect R₂ = 20 kΩ in parallel with R₁ for a further 5.00 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b)(i) τ₁ = R₁C = 18.00 s, so V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁) = 5.134 V ≈ 5.13 V (confirming 5.1 V). (b)(ii) R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 15.0 kΩ, giving τ₂ = R_eq C = 4.500 s ≈ 4.50 s. (b)(iii) V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂) = 1.690 V ≈ 1.69 V. (b)(iv) larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

markScheme.criterion: Mentions charge stored per unit potential difference (coulombs per volt).
Complete SI unit definition: capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Evaluates stage-1 time constant τ₁ = R₁C = 18.0 s.
Correctly substitutes V₀, t₁, and τ₁ into V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁).
Shows V₁ = 5.134 V (≥3 s.f.: 5.13 V), clearly matching 5.1 V.
Combines R₁ || R₂ = 15.0 kΩ and calculates τ₂ = R_eq C = 4.50 s.
Substitutes V₁ (accepting rounded prompt value on ECF), t₂, and τ₂ into V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂).
Correct final potential difference V₂ = 1.69 V.
States correctly that V₂ would be larger (smaller/larger matching direction).
Explains via time constants in both stages: larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

parts.prompt: Define the farad.
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the unit definition linking electric charge in coulombs and potential difference in volts.

parts.prompt: Show clearly that after discharging through R₁ alone for 12.0 s, the potential difference across the capacitor is approximately 5.1 V.
parts.expectedAnswer: 5.134 V (which rounds to 5.13 V and 5.1 V)
workingSteps: Stage 1 time constant τ₁ = R₁ C = (60 × 10³ Ω) × (300 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 18.00 s.
Substitute into V₁ = V₀ exp(−t₁ / τ₁) = 10.00 V × exp(−12 / 18.00 s).
Evaluate to 4 s.f.: V₁ = 5.134 V ≈ 5.13 V (confirming approximately 5.1 V).

parts.prompt: At the instant Switch C closes, calculate the new time constant τ₂ of the discharge circuit.
workingSteps: Combined parallel resistance R_eq = (R₁ R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (60 × 20) / (60 + 20) = 15.0 kΩ.
New time constant τ₂ = R_eq C = (15 × 10³ Ω) × (300 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 4.500 s ≈ 4.50 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference V₂ across the capacitor after a further 5.00 s with both Switch B and Switch C closed.
workingSteps: Start Stage 2 decay from V₁ = 5.134 V with time constant τ₂ = 4.500 s.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how the final potential difference V₂ would change if resistor R₁ were replaced by a larger resistor throughout the entire experiment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing the first resistor with a larger resistor gives a larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.
workingSteps: A larger resistance changes both the initial discharge time constant and the combined parallel resistance in the same direction.
Link the altered time constants in both stages to the rate of exponential decay and the remaining potential difference.

items.stem: During a charge-conservation test on an isolated laboratory capacitor bank, C₁ = 15 μF at initial voltage V₁ = 47 V is connected by closing switch S across C₂ = 45 μF (initially uncharged). What final common potential difference is established across both capacitors?
items.workedSolution: Total conserved charge Q_net = C₁V₁ + C₂V₂ = 7.05 × 10⁻⁴ C. Final parallel capacitance C_eq = 60 μF, so V_f = Q_net / (C₁ + C₂) = 11.8 V.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves net charge Q_net and divides by C₁ + C₂ to obtain 11.8 V (D).

options.text: A rotating X-ray tube measures exponential photon attenuation across an opposing ring of detectors.
options.distractorRationale: That describes a CT scanner rather than an MR scanner.

options.label: B
options.text: Piezoelectric crystals detect ultrasound echoes reflected from acoustic impedance boundaries.
options.distractorRationale: That describes medical ultrasound B-scanning.

options.label: C
options.text: Successive short radio frequency pulses excite proton spin states and emitted RF signals on de-excitation build the image after detection by the receiver coils.

options.label: D
options.text: A gamma camera counts 140 keV gamma photons emitted by an injected technetium tracer.
options.distractorRationale: That describes radionuclide scintigraphy rather than MRI.

items.stem: An engineer calibrates a microbalance displacement detector built from parallel plates of area 1.1 m² separated by 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m of fused quartz wafer whose relative permittivity is 6. With 320 V connected steadily between the plates and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹,

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into C = εᵣε₀A / d.
Obtains 9.74 × 10⁻⁸ F.
Multiplies capacitance from (a) by applied voltage Q = CV.
Obtains 3.12 × 10⁻⁵ C.
Applies U = ½CV² using capacitance from (a).
Obtains 4.98 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: During field ramping in a plasma-tokamak diagnostic flux loop (400 turns, area 0.005 m², resistance 16 Ω), a uniform magnetic field directed at an angle of 65° with the normal to the coil ramps uniformly from 0.36 T to 1.08 T over 0.05 s. What is the magnitude of the average emf induced in the coil?

markScheme.criterion: Projects flux along coil normal (65°) and evaluates |ε| = N|ΔΦ|/Δt = 12.2 V (D).

options.distractorRationale: Introduces an extraneous factor of one-half during algebraic rearrangement.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the number of turns N in Faraday's law |ε| = N|ΔΦ|/Δt.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses sin 65° instead of cos 65° when projecting B along the coil normal.

items.stem: Accelerated from rest through 2200 V in a secondary-ion mass analyser magnet, a doubly ionised magnesium ion of charge +3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 3.98 × 10⁻²⁶ kg passes into a uniform 0.320 T magnetic field directed out of the page at right angles to its velocity.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ½mv² = |q|V_acc to solve for v.
Obtains 1.88 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
Applies r = mv / (|q|B) using v from (a).
Obtains 0.0731 m.
Multiplies orbital radius from (b) by two.
Obtains 0.146 m.

items.stem: In a dielectric displacement gauge, parallel plates of area 0.35 m² separated by 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ m with dielectric relative permittivity 5.5 are initially charged to 350 V (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹). The capacitor is disconnected from the DC source so the plates remain electrically isolated, and the plate separation is then adjusted to 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ m (maintaining relative permittivity 5.5).

markScheme.criterion: Finds initial C = εᵣε₀A/d and applies U_i = ½CV².
Obtains 4.35 × 10⁻³ J.
Evaluates C′ = εᵣε₀A / d′ at the new separation.
Obtains 3.55 × 10⁻⁸ F.
Uses constant charge U_f = Q²/(2C′) and subtracts U_i.
Obtains 4.35 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: Across a regulated 23 V rail in a camera strobe flash bank, capacitor C₁ (24 μF) is placed in series with capacitor C₂ (48 μF). What potential difference is developed across capacitor C₁?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent capacitance C_eq = 1.60 × 10⁻⁵ F, so series charge Q = C_eq V₀ = 3.68 × 10⁻⁴ C. Across C₁, V₁ = Q / C₁ = 15.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds common series charge Q and computes V₁ = Q/C₁ = 15.3 V (B).

items.stem: Magnetic flux of density 0.640 T (directed out of the page) pervades the vacuum region of a space-radiation geomagnetic trap simulator where a proton of mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C circulates at constant speed 3.40 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ normal to the field lines.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = |q|vB / m.
Obtains 2.08 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻².
Uses r = v² / a_c (= mv / |q|B).
Obtains 0.0554 m.
Uses f = |q|B / (2πm) (= v / 2πr).
Obtains 9.76 × 10⁶ Hz.

items.stem: A radio-frequency linear accelerator operating at 32.0 MHz accelerates protons from rest across successive 60.0 kV gaps ($m_p = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$). Consider a proton entering the 5th drift tube.
items.workedSolution: (a) E_k = 300 keV. (b) v₅ = 7.58 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. (c) L₅ = 11.8 cm. (d) drift tubes increase in length proportional to the square root of tube number so faster particles still spend exactly half an alternating period inside each shielded tube.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates E_k = 5 × 60.0 = 300 keV.
Converts keV to joules and applies v = √(2E_k/m_p).
Obtains speed v₅ = 7.58 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
Applies L = v / (2f) using half an RF period.
Obtains drift-tube length L₅ = 11.8 cm.
States RF supply has fixed frequency so polarity flips every T/2.

Links higher speed √n to proportionally longer tube length (drift tubes increase in length proportional to the square root of tube number so faster particles still spend exactly half an alternating period inside each shielded tube).

items.workedSolution: (a) C_p = 45 μF, C_eq = 30.00 μF ≈ 30.0 μF. (b) The parallel pair of capacitors hits 50 V first, giving V_AB,max = 75.00 V ≈ 75.0 V. (c) E_max = ½ C_eq V_AB,max² = 0.08437 J ≈ 0.0844 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the combined capacitance of the network between A and B in μF.
workingSteps: Parallel branch: C_p = C₂ + C₃ = 20 + 25 = 45 μF.
Series combination: C_eq = (C₁ C_p) / (C₁ + C_p) = (90 × 45) / (90 + 45) = 30.00 μF ≈ 30.0 μF.

parts.prompt: Determine the maximum safe potential difference that can be applied across A and B, stating which section reaches its voltage rating first.
parts.expectedAnswer: 75.0 V (limited by the parallel pair of capacitors)
workingSteps: In series both sections hold equal charge Q, so V ∝ 1/C; the smaller capacitance (parallel pair of capacitors) reaches 50 V first.
Maximum safe total pd V_AB,max = 50 × (1 + 45 / 90) = 75.00 V ≈ 75.0 V.

options.distractorRationale: Frequency stays locked to the 50 Hz AC field; rotation scales amplitude by cos θ.

options.label: C
options.text: Peak-to-peak voltage is maximum when the coil plane is perpendicular to B (normal parallel to B, θ = 0°), and a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

options.label: D
options.text: Using a DC battery in the large coil gives a clearer steady horizontal line on the CRO proportional to B.
options.distractorRationale: Static DC induces zero emf in a stationary search coil.

items.stem: In a sensor low-pass RC network, a 80 μF capacitor initially charged to 15 V begins discharging through a 20 kΩ resistor when switch S closes, and a sensor samples the circuit after 2.88 s. What is the potential difference across the capacitor at t = 2.88 s?
items.workedSolution: Time constant τ = RC = 1.60 s. For discharging, V_C(2.88 s) = 15 e^(−2.88/1.60) = 2.48 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds τ = RC and evaluates V_C at t = 2.88 s to obtain 2.48 V (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides elapsed time t by half-time RC ln 2 instead of the RC time constant τ = RC in the exponent.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the charging equation V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)) instead of exponential discharge V₀e^(−t/RC).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the capacitor reaches or retains the full supply voltage V₀ instantaneously.

items.stem: A filament lamp glows with identical steady brightness when powered by a 12 V DC battery or by an AC supply of peak voltage 17.0 V. Why do the two supplies deliver equal heating?
items.workedSolution: Since 17.0 / √2 ≈ 12.0 V, root mean square potential difference equals the steady direct potential difference that dissipates the same mean power in a given resistor. Therefore the correct statement is: Because the AC supply's root mean square potential difference equals the steady direct potential difference that dissipates the same mean power in a given resistor

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: root mean square potential difference equals the steady direct potential difference that dissipates the same mean power in a given resistor.

options.label: A
options.text: Because alternating current reverses direction so half the energy cancels out, making peak voltage equal to DC voltage.
options.distractorRationale: Heating P = V²/R is positive on both half-cycles; mean power equals half peak power, so V_rms = V₀/√2.

options.label: B
options.text: Because filament resistance doubles automatically whenever alternating current is applied.
options.distractorRationale: At identical brightness and temperature, filament resistance is the same.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the AC supply's root mean square potential difference equals the steady direct potential difference that dissipates the same mean power in a given resistor

options.label: D
options.text: Because DC current heats only during positive intervals whereas AC heats continuously.
options.distractorRationale: DC heats continuously at constant rate V_DC²/R.

items.stem: Why is magnetically soft iron preferred over magnetically hard steel for the core of an AC transformer?
items.workedSolution: A laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage. Therefore the correct statement is: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily every cycle: a laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage

options.label: A
options.text: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily every cycle: a laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage

options.label: B
options.text: Soft iron remains permanently magnetised so the transformer continues outputting AC even when the primary supply is disconnected.
options.distractorRationale: Permanent magnetisation is hard steel, which causes severe hysteresis energy loss.

options.label: C
options.text: Soft iron is an electrical insulator so zero eddy currents can ever be induced inside a solid block.
options.distractorRationale: Iron is a metallic conductor; laminations are still required to restrict eddy currents.

options.label: D
options.text: Soft iron prevents magnetic flux from reversing direction so the secondary coil outputs steady DC.
options.distractorRationale: Changing flux is essential for induction; soft iron makes rapid flux reversal low-loss.

items.stem: A coastal wind-farm substation steps 11.0 kV generator output up for regional grid transmission along cables of total resistance 6.00 Ω. The transformer has Nₚ = 600 primary turns, Nₛ = 6000 secondary turns, and primary voltage Vₚ = 1.10 × 10⁴ V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vₛ = 1.10 × 10⁵ V. (b) Iₚ = 189 A. (c) P_loss = 1.94 × 10⁵ W. (d) thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates Vₛ = 1.10 × 10⁵ V.
Applies η = (Iₛ Vₛ) / (Iₚ Vₚ).
Obtains Iₚ = 189 A.
Finds cable current I = P / Vₛ = 180 A.
Calculates cable loss P_loss = I²R = 1.94 × 10⁵ W.
States insulating layers between iron sheets increase resistance to eddy currents.
Links smaller eddy currents to reduced I²R core heating (thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core).

parts.prompt: Calculate the secondary output voltage Vₛ assuming negligible flux leakage.
When the transformer operates at 95% efficiency delivering secondary current 18.0 A, calculate the primary current Iₚ.
If power 1.98 × 10⁷ W is transmitted at voltage Vₛ along cables of total resistance 6.00 Ω, calculate the thermal power dissipated in the cables.
Explain how laminating the soft-iron core reduces internal thermal energy losses in the transformer.
parts.expectedAnswer: Laminating the core works because thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.
workingSteps: thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

items.stem: Students record the sinusoidal output of a rotating search-coil generator connected across a 15.0 Ω test resistor on an oscilloscope. The oscilloscope is set to Y-gain 1.00 V div⁻¹ and time-base 4.00 ms div⁻¹. The sinusoidal trace spans 6.00 divisions peak-to-peak and 2.50 horizontal divisions per complete cycle.
items.workedSolution: (a) V_rms = 2.12 V. (b) f = 100 Hz. (c) P_mean = 0.300 W. (d) switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Finds peak voltage V₀ = 3.00 V by halving peak-to-peak height.
Divides by √2 to obtain V_rms = 2.12 V.
Calculates period T = 0.0100 s.
Inverts T to obtain f = 100 Hz.
Evaluates P_mean = V_rms² / R = 0.300 W.
States horizontal deflection ceases so spot oscillates vertically at the centre.
States full length equals peak-to-peak voltage (switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage).

parts.prompt: Calculate the root-mean-square potential difference V_rms across the resistor.
Determine the frequency f of the alternating supply.
Calculate the mean power dissipated in the load resistor.
Describe and explain what appears on the oscilloscope screen if the time-base is switched OFF.
parts.expectedAnswer: With no horizontal sweep, switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.
workingSteps: Without horizontal deflection the electron beam moves purely vertically between +V₀ and −V₀.
switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

items.stem: A student investigates how magnetic flux linkage $N\Phi = B A N \cos\theta$ varies with angle $\theta$ using a rotatable search coil mounted at the centre of a large 50 Hz AC circular coil connected to an oscilloscope.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Power the large circular/Helmholtz coil from a 50 Hz AC supply with a series ammeter so rms current (and hence peak flux density B) stays constant throughout. Clamp the rotatable search coil securely at the exact geometric centre of the large coil where the magnetic field is uniform. Rotate the search coil until the CRO shows maximum peak-to-peak vertical deflection (coil plane perpendicular to B, defining θ = 0°), and align the protractor pointer while viewing vertically from above to avoid parallax. Switch the CRO time-base OFF (displaying a crisp vertical bar of length V_pp) and choose a sensitive Y-gain filling most of the graticule to cut percentage uncertainty. Record V_pp every 10° from 0° to 90°, repeating readings while rotating back to reduce random error. Plot V_pp against cos θ: a straight best-fit line through the origin verifies NΦ = BAN cos θ, and its gradient equals 4πfBAN, yielding B = gradient / (4πfAN). Finally, note that a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

markScheme.criterion: Maintains constant AC frequency and constant coil current (monitored with an ammeter) and positions search coil at the uniform centre.
Defines θ = 0° cleanly (coil plane perpendicular to B / maximum V_pp) and reads protractor directly from above to avoid parallax.
Optimises CRO Y-gain to fill screen (and optionally switches time-base OFF to measure vertical V_pp accurately).
Measures V_pp across at least six angles from 0° to 90°, taking repeat readings to reduce random error.
Plots V_pp against cos θ (straight line through origin confirms cos θ dependence) and computes B = gradient / (4πfAN).
Contrasts sensors clearly: a search coil requires changing/AC magnetic flux whereas a Hall probe measures static DC magnetic fields.

parts.prompt: Describe a complete experimental procedure to verify the $\cos\theta$ relationship and determine the peak flux density $B$, including alignment, CRO settings, angle measurement precautions, graphical analysis, and contrast with a Hall probe. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Keep the AC coil current and frequency constant using a series ammeter, centre the search coil in the uniform field region, align θ = 0° at peak CRO voltage while reading the protractor directly from above to avoid parallax, switch time-base off or optimise Y-gain to record V_pp from 0° to 90° in 10° steps, plot V_pp against cos θ to confirm linearity and extract B = gradient / (4πfAN), noting that a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.
workingSteps: Level 1: Keep AC frequency and rms current constant; centre search coil rigidly on axis inside large coil where field is uniform.

Level 2: Locate θ = 0° (maximum V_pp, coil plane perpendicular to B); view protractor directly from above (or use set square) to prevent parallax; adjust Y-gain (and time-base OFF) for maximum vertical span.
Level 3: Measure V_pp at >= 7 angles (0° to 90°), plot V_pp vs cos θ (straight line through origin), extract B = grad / (4πfAN), and contrast AC search coil vs DC Hall probe.

items.stem: A student is given a 0.01 g digital top-pan balance, a U-shaped steel yoke holding two opposite slab magnets, a stiff straight copper rod, a variable DC power supply, a rheostat, an ammeter, and a millimetre ruler.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Mount opposite poles (N facing S) on the steel yoke atop a 0.01 g top-pan balance. Clamp the stiff horizontal copper rod securely in a retort stand so it passes straight and perpendicular to the magnetic field lines without touching the magnets or yoke. Wire the rod in series with a DC supply, switch, variable resistor, and digital ammeter. Measure the active length L of the magnets with a Vernier calliper or ruler. Press TARE with zero current (or note the untared mass M₀). Increase current I in at least six even steps (e.g. 0.5 A to 4.5 A), recording Δm and I quickly while opening the switch between readings so the copper rod does not overheat or burn fingers. By Newton's 3rd law, the upward magnetic force BIl on the rod exerts an equal downward force on the magnet yoke, giving Δm·g = BIl. Plot Δm (in kg) against I (in A) for a straight line through the origin (or M vs I with intercept M₀), calculate gradient from a > 50% triangle, and evaluate B = (gradient × 9.81) / L.

markScheme.criterion: Clamps stiff copper wire horizontally perpendicular to magnetic field lines without touching the magnet yoke or balance.
Connects DC supply, variable resistor, ammeter, and switch in series; limits current / switches off between readings to prevent wire overheating.
Measures active magnet length L with a ruler/Vernier callipers and tares balance at I = 0 (or notes untared intercept M₀).
Records balance mass reading across at least six currents (repeating and averaging to reduce random error).
Explains via Newton's 3rd law that an equal opposite downward force acts on the magnet yoke so Δm·g = BIl.
Plots Δm (or M) against I, takes gradient using > 50% span, converts grams to kg, and obtains B = (gradient × 9.81) / L.

parts.prompt: Describe a complete experimental procedure to determine the magnetic flux density $B$ between the slab magnets graphically, explaining setup, alignment, safety, measurements, Newton's third law, and analysis. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Place the magnet yoke on the 0.01 g balance, clamp the stiff copper rod horizontally and perpendicular to B without touching the yoke, tare the balance at zero current (or record untared intercept M₀), vary current I in six steps with a rheostat while switching off between readings to prevent rod heating; by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current; plot Δm (or M) against I and compute B = (gradient × 9.81) / L using magnet length L.
workingSteps: Level 1: Clamp stiff copper rod horizontally perpendicular to uniform B without touching magnets; series DC supply, rheostat, ammeter, switch.
Level 2: Measure active magnet length L with ruler/callipers; tare balance at I = 0; step current across >= 6 values, opening switch between readings so wire stays cool.
Level 3: Explain N3L downward force on yoke -> Δm g = BIl, plot Δm (or M) vs I, extract B = (gradient × g) / L (converting g to kg).

items.stem: The cutaway schematic shows a step-up power transformer constructed with a laminated soft-iron closed core and thick copper coils.
items.workedSolution: laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage. A laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage. Specifically: (1) Alternating core flux induces circulating eddy currents in the conducting iron; slicing the core into thin laminations separated by insulating varnish increases electrical resistance across eddy-current paths, reducing eddy current magnitude and I²R core heating. (2) Repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation every AC cycle dissipates hysteresis heat; magnetically soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily with a narrow hysteresis loop. (3) Current in primary and secondary windings causes copper I²R heating; thick low-resistivity copper wire lowers winding resistance. (4) Incomplete flux linkage loses energy; a closed overlapping soft-iron core channels almost all primary magnetic flux through the secondary coil.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains that alternating magnetic flux induces circulating eddy currents inside the conducting iron core causing I²R heating.
L1b: Explains that laminating the core (thin iron sheets separated by insulating layers) increases resistance to eddy-current loops, lowering eddy current heating.
L2a: Identifies hysteresis loss from repeated magnetisation/demagnetisation of the core every AC cycle.
L2b: States magnetically soft iron is used because it magnetises and demagnetises easily with minimal hysteresis energy loss.
L3a: Identifies resistive I²R heating in the windings and explains using thick, low-resistivity copper wire to reduce resistance.
L3b: Identifies magnetic flux leakage and explains using a closed soft-iron core (or overlapping coils on one limb) so nearly all flux links the secondary coil.

parts.prompt: Explain the four main sources of energy loss in a practical AC transformer and detail how each physical design feature minimises those losses to achieve efficiencies exceeding 95%.
parts.expectedAnswer: laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage. A laminated soft-iron core with insulating layers increases resistance to reduce eddy current heating, soft iron lowers hysteresis loss, thick copper coils cut resistive heating, and a closed core minimises flux leakage. Specifically: (1) Alternating core flux induces circulating eddy currents in the conducting iron; slicing the core into thin laminations separated by insulating varnish increases electrical resistance across eddy-current paths, reducing eddy current magnitude and I²R core heating. (2) Repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation every AC cycle dissipates hysteresis heat; magnetically soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily with a narrow hysteresis loop. (3) Current in primary and secondary windings causes copper I²R heating; thick low-resistivity copper wire lowers winding resistance. (4) Incomplete flux linkage loses energy; a closed overlapping soft-iron core channels almost all primary magnetic flux through the secondary coil.
workingSteps: L1: Eddy currents in core → thin laminations with insulating varnish layers raise resistance to lower I²R core heating.
L2: Hysteresis loss → magnetically soft iron; Copper winding loss → thick low-resistivity copper wire.
L3: Flux leakage → closed core / overlapping windings on same limb for near-complete flux linkage.

items.stem: A bar magnet is released from rest (north pole downward) above a vertical solenoid connected to a centre-zero galvanometer, producing the asymmetric bipolar emf-time trace shown (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy. As the north pole enters, flux linkage increases and by Lenz's law a north pole is induced at the top of the coil to repel and oppose approach; at the midpoint flux linkage is maximum so dΦ/dt = 0 and ε = 0; as the magnet exits, flux linkage decreases so the induced current reverses to produce a north pole at the bottom attracting the departing south pole. Because gravity accelerates the magnet, it exits faster than it enters, giving a larger rate of change of flux linkage (taller peak emf) over a shorter duration, while both pulses have equal enclosed area |∫ε dt| = NΦ. Overall, the induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy; if the induced pole assisted the motion, the magnet would accelerate while generating electrical power, creating energy from nothing.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States that as the N pole approaches, increasing flux linkage induces a current creating a N pole at the top of the coil to repel the magnet.
L1b: States that at the midpoint dΦ/dt = 0 so ε = 0, and on exit decreasing flux reverses current polarity to attract and oppose departure.
L2a: Explains exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because gravity accelerates the magnet, increasing dΦ/dt.
L2b: Explains both pulses enclose equal area because total change in flux linkage NΦ on entry equals NΦ on exit.
L3a: Links opposition to energy conservation: mechanical work / loss of GPE done against opposing magnetic force converts into electrical/thermal energy (I²Rt).
L3b: Explains the contradiction: if induced polarity assisted motion, the magnet would accelerate while producing electrical energy, violating conservation of energy.

items.stem: Medical cyclotrons accelerate protons to produce short-lived PET radioisotopes using two hollow D-shaped metal dees placed in an evacuated chamber between the poles of a large electromagnet.
items.workedSolution: a perpendicular magnetic field bends ions into semicircular arcs inside hollow D-shaped dees while an alternating potential difference of constant frequency f = BQ / (2 pi m) accelerates them across the gap every half-revolution until they exit at maximum radius. Protons enter near the centre and are accelerated across the narrow gap by the alternating electric field, gaining kinetic energy Q V_gap per crossing. Inside the hollow metal dees the electric field is zero, while the uniform perpendicular magnetic field exerts a centripetal force BQv = mv²/r, bending protons into semicircular paths of radius r = mv/(BQ) without changing their speed. The time in each dee is t = πr/v = πm/(BQ), independent of both v and r. Hence a constant RF frequency f = 1/(2t) = BQ/(2πm) reverses polarity every half-revolution to keep protons accelerating outward until exiting at radius R with v_max = BQR/m and E_k(max) = B²Q²R²/(2m) (limited at high energy by relativistic mass increase).

markScheme.criterion: L1: States that ions are accelerated by the electric field across the gap between the hollow metal dees (where E = 0 inside).
L1: States that the perpendicular magnetic field provides centripetal force BQv = mv²/r, bending ions in semicircles without doing work.
L2: Derives r = mv/(BQ), showing orbit radius increases proportionally with speed after each gap crossing.
L2: Derives semicircular transit time t = πr/v = πm/(BQ) and shows v and r cancel out.
L3: Deduces constant RF alternating frequency f = BQ/(2πm) so polarity reverses synchronously every half-revolution.
L3: Relates maximum exit kinetic energy E_k = B²Q²R²/(2m) to dee radius R and field B (and optionally notes relativistic frequency mismatch at very high energy).

parts.prompt: Explain the physical operation of a cyclotron, deriving the required alternating supply frequency f = BQ / (2πm), explaining why the frequency remains constant as proton speed increases, and showing how exit radius R and field B set maximum exit kinetic energy. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: a perpendicular magnetic field bends ions into semicircular arcs inside hollow D-shaped dees while an alternating potential difference of constant frequency f = BQ / (2 pi m) accelerates them across the gap every half-revolution until they exit at maximum radius. Protons enter near the centre and are accelerated across the narrow gap by the alternating electric field, gaining kinetic energy Q V_gap per crossing. Inside the hollow metal dees the electric field is zero, while the uniform perpendicular magnetic field exerts a centripetal force BQv = mv²/r, bending protons into semicircular paths of radius r = mv/(BQ) without changing their speed. The time in each dee is t = πr/v = πm/(BQ), independent of both v and r. Hence a constant RF frequency f = 1/(2t) = BQ/(2πm) reverses polarity every half-revolution to keep protons accelerating outward until exiting at radius R with v_max = BQR/m and E_k(max) = B²Q²R²/(2m) (limited at high energy by relativistic mass increase).
workingSteps: Describe hollow D-dees (E = 0 inside), perpendicular uniform B providing centripetal force BQv = mv²/r.
Explain alternating RF p.d. across gap doing work Q V_gap every half-turn.
Derive half-period t = πr/v = πm/(BQ) independent of speed, giving constant f = BQ/(2πm).
Derive exit speed v = BQR/m and E_k = B²Q²R²/(2m), noting relativistic limit at very high speeds.

items.stem: During isotopic analysis on a cosmochemistry meteorite isotope separator, magnesium ions (q = +3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m₁ = 3.98 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, m₂ = 4.32 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) traverse a velocity selector with E = 9.60 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B₁ = 0.35 T and strike a photographic detector wall after semicircular deflection in B₂ = 0.7 T (out of the page). How far from the entry slit S does the lighter isotope strike the detector wall?
items.workedSolution: v = E / B₁ = 2.74 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ and r₁ = m₁v / (qB₂) = 0.0487 m. Strike distance from slit S is D₁ = 2r₁ = 0.0975 m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes D₁ = 2r₁ = 2m₁E / (qB₁B₂) = 0.0975 m (C).

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Reports the orbital radius r₁ rather than the semicircular chord distance D₁ = 2r₁ from slit S.

items.stem: In the slow-fast capacitor test unit shown, a capacitor of capacitance C = 500 μF is first fully charged to V₀ = 6.00 V by closing Switch A while Switches B and C remain open. Switch A is then opened and Switch B is closed so the capacitor discharges through R₁ = 60 kΩ for 18.0 s. At t = 18.0 s, while Switch B stays closed, Switch C is closed to connect R₂ = 30 kΩ in parallel with R₁ for a further 9.00 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b)(i) τ₁ = R₁C = 30.00 s, so V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁) = 3.293 V ≈ 3.29 V (confirming 3.3 V). (b)(ii) R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 20.0 kΩ, giving τ₂ = R_eq C = 10.00 s ≈ 10.0 s. (b)(iii) V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂) = 1.339 V ≈ 1.34 V. (b)(iv) larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

markScheme.criterion: Mentions charge stored per unit potential difference (coulombs per volt).
Complete SI unit definition: capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Evaluates stage-1 time constant τ₁ = R₁C = 30.0 s.
Correctly substitutes V₀, t₁, and τ₁ into V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁).
Shows V₁ = 3.293 V (≥3 s.f.: 3.29 V), clearly matching 3.3 V.
Combines R₁ || R₂ = 20.0 kΩ and calculates τ₂ = R_eq C = 10.0 s.
Substitutes V₁ (accepting rounded prompt value on ECF), t₂, and τ₂ into V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂).
Correct final potential difference V₂ = 1.34 V.
States correctly that V₂ would be larger (smaller/larger matching direction).
Explains via time constants in both stages: larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

parts.prompt: Define the farad.
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the unit definition linking electric charge in coulombs and potential difference in volts.

parts.prompt: Show clearly that after discharging through R₁ alone for 18.0 s, the potential difference across the capacitor is approximately 3.3 V.
parts.expectedAnswer: 3.293 V (which rounds to 3.29 V and 3.3 V)
workingSteps: Stage 1 time constant τ₁ = R₁ C = (60 × 10³ Ω) × (500 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 30.00 s.
Substitute into V₁ = V₀ exp(−t₁ / τ₁) = 6.000 V × exp(−18 / 30.00 s).
Evaluate to 4 s.f.: V₁ = 3.293 V ≈ 3.29 V (confirming approximately 3.3 V).

parts.prompt: At the instant Switch C closes, calculate the new time constant τ₂ of the discharge circuit.
workingSteps: Combined parallel resistance R_eq = (R₁ R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (60 × 30) / (60 + 30) = 20.0 kΩ.
New time constant τ₂ = R_eq C = (20 × 10³ Ω) × (500 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 10.00 s ≈ 10.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference V₂ across the capacitor after a further 9.00 s with both Switch B and Switch C closed.
workingSteps: Start Stage 2 decay from V₁ = 3.293 V with time constant τ₂ = 10.00 s.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how the final potential difference V₂ would change if resistor R₁ were replaced by a larger resistor throughout the entire experiment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing the first resistor with a larger resistor gives a larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.
workingSteps: A larger resistance changes both the initial discharge time constant and the combined parallel resistance in the same direction.
Link the altered time constants in both stages to the rate of exponential decay and the remaining potential difference.

items.stem: After disconnecting its charging cell in an isolated laboratory capacitor bank, capacitor C₁ = 10 μF at V₁ = 47 V shares charge across switch S with C₂ = 30 μF, which is initially uncharged.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Q_net = C₁V₁ + C₂V₂ before switch closure.
Obtains 4.70 × 10⁻⁴ C.
Divides conserved charge from (a) by C₁ + C₂.
Obtains 11.8 V.
Subtracts final stored energy ½(C₁ + C₂)V_f² from initial stored energy.
Obtains 8.28 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: In a crossed-field apparatus, a plate pd of 1200 V across a 5.00 cm separation balances a magnetic flux density of 1.60 mT. When the electric field is switched off, the same magnetic field bends the beam into a circular arc of radius 5.33 cm. What value of $e/m$ is obtained?
items.workedSolution: $E = \frac{1200}{0.0500} = 2.40 \times 10^4\text{ V m}^{-1}$. Using $v = E/B$ in $e/m = v/(Br)$ gives $\frac{e}{m} = \frac{E}{B^2 r} = \frac{2.40 \times 10^4}{(1.60 \times 10^{-3})^2 \times 0.0533} = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A high-field $3.00\text{ T}$ MR scanner excites water protons precessing according to $f = (42.6\text{ MHz T}^{-1}) B_0$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f = 128 MHz$. (b) $E = hf / e = 5.30 × 10⁻⁷ eV$, vastly below ionisation energies (~10 eV). (c) MRI provides high soft-tissue contrast using non-ionising radio frequency radiation excludes ferromagnetic implants and pacemakers.

markScheme.criterion: Correct frequency 128 MHz.
Applies $E = hf$ and divides by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$.
Correct photon energy 5.30 × 10⁻⁷ eV.
Notes photon energy is millions of times smaller than atomic ionisation energy.
States non-ionising radio frequency radiation excludes ferromagnetic implants and pacemakers.
Notes superior soft-tissue contrast compared with CT.

items.stem: A potential difference of 1200 V in the source stage of a sputter-source magnetic momentum filter accelerates a singly ionised lithium ion of mass 1.16 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C from rest into a perpendicular magnetic sector of flux density 0.450 T (into the page). What speed does the particle reach upon entering the magnetic field?
items.workedSolution: Equating ½mv² = |q|V_acc gives v = √(2|q|V_acc / m) = √(2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1200 / 1.16 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) = 1.82 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = √(2|q|V_acc / m) = 1.82 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 4 instead of 2 inside the square root.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes v² = 2|q|V_acc / m without taking the square root.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the ½ in ½mv² = |q|V_acc and computes √(|q|V_acc / m).

items.stem: An experimental parallel-plate laboratory condenser features plates of area 0.35 m² at initial spacing 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m filled with a medium of relative permittivity 3.5 and charged to 350 V (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹). The plates are disconnected from the DC source so the plates remain electrically isolated, and the plate separation is then adjusted to 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m while εᵣ stays at 3.5. What is the new potential difference across the isolated plates?
items.workedSolution: For isolated plates, charge Q is conserved while C′ = C₀(d/d′). Therefore V′ = Q / C′ = V₀(d′/d) = 350 × (0.00025 / 0.0005) = 175 V.

markScheme.criterion: Uses charge conservation V′ = V₀(d′/d) to obtain 175 V (D).

items.stem: Two capacitors rated C₁ = 12 μF and C₂ = 36 μF are wired end-to-end in series across an ideal 17 V terminal supply on a DC rail smoothing subcircuit.

markScheme.criterion: Applies reciprocal series rule 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
Obtains 9.00 × 10⁻⁶ F.
Uses Q = C_eq V₀ and V₁ = Q / C₁.
Obtains 12.8 V.
Applies U = ½C_eq V₀².
Obtains 1.30 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: A uniform 0.480 T magnetic field (directed out of the page) fills a medical radioisotope cyclotron chamber. Entering at right angles to the field with speed 4.50 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, a single proton of charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg curves along a circular trajectory. If the particle completes a semicircular turn to strike a flat detector wall on the entry plane, how far from the entry slit does it hit?
items.workedSolution: Cyclotron radius r = mv / (|q|B) = 0.0979 m. Across a semicircular turn, the impact distance from the entry slit equals the orbit diameter D = 2r = 0.196 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds r = mv/(|q|B) and doubles to diameter D = 2r = 0.196 m (B).

items.stem: Protons ($m_p = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$) enter a 40.0 MHz linear accelerator from rest and pass through 4 accelerating gaps, each of peak potential difference 50.0 kV. Using $L_n = \frac{1}{2f}\sqrt{2neV/m_p}$, calculate the required length $L_4$ of the fourth drift tube in centimetres.

markScheme.criterion: Applies L_n = (1/(2f))√(2neV/m_p) to obtain 7.73 cm.

items.stem: In an electron-microscope Wien monochromator, parallel plates separated by 0.02 m are held at 320 V (upper plate negative) perpendicular to a uniform 0.12 T magnetic field (out of the page). A proton (charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is injected horizontally to the right at 8.00 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹. At what speed would a proton instead have to enter this same selector to pass straight through undeflected?
items.workedSolution: Electric field E = V / d = 320 / 0.02 = 1.60 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Undeflected transmission requires qvB = qE, giving v_sel = E / B = 1.33 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_sel = V / (Bd) = 1.33 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: In the inverter DC-link module shown between terminals A and B, capacitor C₁ = 200 μF is connected in series with the parallel pair C₂ = 40 μF and C₃ = 60 μF. Every capacitor has a maximum safe working voltage of 60 V. What is the maximum safe potential difference that can be applied across terminals A and B without exceeding the rating of any capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel pair C_p = C₂ + C₃ = 100 μF. Because C₁ (200 μF) and C_p (100 μF) carry equal series charge Q, the smaller capacitance (parallel pair of capacitors) reaches 60 V first. Thus V_AB,max = 60 × (1 + 100 / 200) = 90.00 V ≈ 90.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the parallel pair of capacitors limits the voltage and calculates V_AB,max = 90.0 V.

items.stem: In Required Practical 11, a search coil with $N = 3000$ turns of area 1.2 cm² is centred inside a large circular coil driven by a 50 Hz AC supply. With the CRO Y-gain set to 100 mV div⁻¹ and the coil normal at $\theta = 25^\circ$ to the field, the peak-to-peak vertical trace spans 5.74 divisions.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 574 mV$. (b) Gradient $= 633 mV$. (c) $B = 2.80 mT$. (d) a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies peak-to-peak divisions by Y-gain.
$V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 574 mV$.
Divides $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ by $\cos 25^\circ$.
Gradient $= 633 mV$.
Applies $V_{\mathrm{pp,max}} = 4\pi f B A N$ with $A$ in m².
Peak flux density $B = 2.80 mT$.
Static DC field gives zero rate of change of flux linkage, so zero induced emf.
Use a Hall probe to measure static DC magnetic flux density.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak-to-peak induced voltage $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ at $\theta = 25^\circ$.
Hence calculate the gradient of the straight-line graph of $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ against $\cos\theta$.
Use $\varepsilon_0 = 2\pi f B A N$ to determine the peak magnetic flux density $B$ in mT.
workingSteps: Gradient $= 4\pi f B A N$, so $B = (633\times 10^{-3}) / (4\pi \times 50 \times 1.2\times 10^{-4} \times 3000) = 2.80 mT$.

parts.prompt: Explain why the search coil fails if the AC supply is replaced by a DC battery, and state what sensor should be used instead.
parts.expectedAnswer: a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density
workingSteps: Faraday's law requires rate of change of flux linkage d(NΦ)/dt ≠ 0, which is zero in static DC.
Use a calibrated Hall probe (perpendicular to field) for static DC flux density.

items.stem: Within a bicycle hub-generator demonstrator, uniform magnetic flux of density 0.35 T links a rotor coil of 80 turns and area 0.01 m² rotating at 60 Hz from maximum flux linkage at t = 0 up to t = 0.00278 s. What is the peak emf ε₀ generated by the rotating coil?
items.workedSolution: Angular speed ω = 2πf = 2π(60) = 377 rad s⁻¹. Peak emf ε₀ = NBAω = 80 × 0.35 × 0.01 × 377 = 106 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε₀ = 2πfNBA to obtain 106 V (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes single-turn peak emf BAω and omits multiplying by N turns.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes rotational frequency f directly into NBAω instead of angular speed ω = 2πf, omitting the 2π factor.

items.stem: In an electrostatic cathode-ray oscilloscope tube, an electron (charge −1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) enters horizontally at 1.40 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ along the midplane between parallel deflecting plates of length 0.04 m and separation 0.05 m maintained at 959 V (neglecting gravity). What is the magnitude of the transverse deflection as the particle exits the plates?
items.workedSolution: Transit time t = L / v₀ = 0.04 / 1.40 × 10⁷ = 2.86 × 10⁻⁹ s. Transverse acceleration a_y = |q|V / (md) = 3.37 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻². Deflection |Δy| = ½ a_y t² = 0.0137 m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates t = L/v₀, a_y = |q|V/(md), and |Δy| = ½a_y t² = 0.0137 m (C).

items.workedSolution: (a) 325 V. (b) 651 V. (c) 4.00 div. (d) with the time-base switched on, applying a steady direct voltage shifts the horizontal trace vertically by a constant distance equal to the potential difference divided by the Y-gain.

Obtains V₀ = 325 V.
Computes V_p-p = 651 V.
Finds period T = 20.0 ms and divides by 5.0 ms div⁻¹.
Obtains 4.00 div.
States steady DC shifts the horizontal line vertically from the 0 V baseline.
States V = vertical divisions × Y-gain setting.

items.stem: A sinusoidal alternating potential difference is displayed cleanly on a cathode-ray oscilloscope screen. What appears on the screen when the time-base control is switched OFF?
items.workedSolution: Without horizontal sweep, the spot moves vertically from +V₀ to −V₀: switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage. Therefore the correct statement is: On the screen, switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage

items.stem: Why is the iron core of a mains power transformer constructed from thin insulated sheets rather than a single solid block of iron?
items.workedSolution: Thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core. Therefore the correct statement is: Because thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

items.stem: A bar magnet is dropped vertically with its north pole pointing downward into a closed solenoid connected to a resistor. What magnetic pole is induced at the top end of the solenoid as the magnet approaches?
items.workedSolution: By Lenz's law, a north pole induced at the top of the coil repelling the approaching north pole opposes the incoming flux change. Therefore the correct statement is: A north pole induced at the top of the coil repelling the approaching north pole

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: north pole induced at the top of the coil repelling the approaching north pole.

options.distractorRationale: Attracting the approaching magnet would violate Lenz's law and energy conservation.

options.distractorRationale: A current-carrying solenoid forms a dipole with opposite poles at its two ends, with the opposing pole at the approach end.

items.stem: A hydroelectric station links its 11.0 kV alternators through a 96.0% efficient step-up transformer to a long-distance 12.0 Ω overhead line. The transformer has Nₚ = 1000 primary turns, Nₛ = 12000 secondary turns, and primary voltage Vₚ = 1.10 × 10⁴ V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vₛ = 1.32 × 10⁵ V. (b) Iₚ = 375 A. (c) P_loss = 4.80 × 10⁵ W. (d) thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates Vₛ = 1.32 × 10⁵ V.
Applies η = (Iₛ Vₛ) / (Iₚ Vₚ).
Obtains Iₚ = 375 A.
Finds cable current I = P / Vₛ = 200 A.
Calculates cable loss P_loss = I²R = 4.80 × 10⁵ W.
States insulating layers between iron sheets increase resistance to eddy currents.
Links smaller eddy currents to reduced I²R core heating (thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core).

When the transformer operates at 96% efficiency delivering secondary current 30.0 A, calculate the primary current Iₚ.
If power 2.64 × 10⁷ W is transmitted at voltage Vₛ along cables of total resistance 12.0 Ω, calculate the thermal power dissipated in the cables.
Explain how laminating the soft-iron core reduces internal thermal energy losses in the transformer.
parts.expectedAnswer: Laminating the core works because thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

items.stem: The secondary output of a lab isolating transformer powers a 50.0 Ω wire-wound resistor monitored on an oscilloscope. The oscilloscope is set to Y-gain 10.0 V div⁻¹ and time-base 5.00 ms div⁻¹. The sinusoidal trace spans 4.00 divisions peak-to-peak and 4.00 horizontal divisions per complete cycle.
items.workedSolution: (a) V_rms = 14.1 V. (b) f = 50.0 Hz. (c) P_mean = 4.00 W. (d) switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Finds peak voltage V₀ = 20.0 V by halving peak-to-peak height.
Divides by √2 to obtain V_rms = 14.1 V.
Calculates period T = 0.0200 s.
Inverts T to obtain f = 50.0 Hz.
Evaluates P_mean = V_rms² / R = 4.00 W.
States horizontal deflection ceases so spot oscillates vertically at the centre.
States full length equals peak-to-peak voltage (switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage).

items.stem: An A-Level physics class compares search-coil induction measurements inside an alternating Helmholtz coil against static field mapping in a direct-current solenoid.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Power the large circular/Helmholtz coil from a 50 Hz AC supply with a series ammeter so rms current (and hence peak flux density B) stays constant throughout. Clamp the rotatable search coil securely at the exact geometric centre of the large coil where the magnetic field is uniform. Rotate the search coil until the CRO shows maximum peak-to-peak vertical deflection (coil plane perpendicular to B, defining θ = 0°), and align the protractor pointer while viewing vertically from above to avoid parallax. Switch the CRO time-base OFF (displaying a crisp vertical bar of length V_pp) and choose a sensitive Y-gain filling most of the graticule to cut percentage uncertainty. Record V_pp every 10° from 0° to 90°, repeating readings while rotating back to reduce random error. Plot V_pp against cos θ: a straight best-fit line through the origin verifies NΦ = BAN cos θ, and its gradient equals 4πfBAN, yielding B = gradient / (4πfAN). Finally, note that a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

markScheme.criterion: Maintains constant AC frequency and constant coil current (monitored with an ammeter) and positions search coil at the uniform centre.
Defines θ = 0° cleanly (coil plane perpendicular to B / maximum V_pp) and reads protractor directly from above to avoid parallax.
Optimises CRO Y-gain to fill screen (and optionally switches time-base OFF to measure vertical V_pp accurately).
Measures V_pp across at least six angles from 0° to 90°, taking repeat readings to reduce random error.
Plots V_pp against cos θ (straight line through origin confirms cos θ dependence) and computes B = gradient / (4πfAN).
Contrasts sensors clearly: a search coil requires changing/AC magnetic flux whereas a Hall probe measures static DC magnetic fields.

parts.prompt: Design an accurate search-coil investigation of flux linkage versus angle $\theta$, detailing how to maintain a constant uniform AC field, minimise reading uncertainty on the CRO and protractor, analyse the graph, and explain when a Hall probe is required. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Keep the AC coil current and frequency constant using a series ammeter, centre the search coil in the uniform field region, align θ = 0° at peak CRO voltage while reading the protractor directly from above to avoid parallax, switch time-base off or optimise Y-gain to record V_pp from 0° to 90° in 10° steps, plot V_pp against cos θ to confirm linearity and extract B = gradient / (4πfAN), noting that a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.
workingSteps: Level 1: Keep AC frequency and rms current constant; centre search coil rigidly on axis inside large coil where field is uniform.

Level 2: Locate θ = 0° (maximum V_pp, coil plane perpendicular to B); view protractor directly from above (or use set square) to prevent parallax; adjust Y-gain (and time-base OFF) for maximum vertical span.
Level 3: Measure V_pp at >= 7 angles (0° to 90°), plot V_pp vs cos θ (straight line through origin), extract B = grad / (4πfAN), and contrast AC search coil vs DC Hall probe.

items.stem: A physics laboratory group investigates how the magnetic force on a straight conductor depends on electric current using a top-pan balance current-balance rig.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Mount opposite poles (N facing S) on the steel yoke atop a 0.01 g top-pan balance. Clamp the stiff horizontal copper rod securely in a retort stand so it passes straight and perpendicular to the magnetic field lines without touching the magnets or yoke. Wire the rod in series with a DC supply, switch, variable resistor, and digital ammeter. Measure the active length L of the magnets with a Vernier calliper or ruler. Press TARE with zero current (or note the untared mass M₀). Increase current I in at least six even steps (e.g. 0.5 A to 4.5 A), recording Δm and I quickly while opening the switch between readings so the copper rod does not overheat or burn fingers. By Newton's 3rd law, the upward magnetic force BIl on the rod exerts an equal downward force on the magnet yoke, giving Δm·g = BIl. Plot Δm (in kg) against I (in A) for a straight line through the origin (or M vs I with intercept M₀), calculate gradient from a > 50% triangle, and evaluate B = (gradient × 9.81) / L.

markScheme.criterion: Clamps stiff copper wire horizontally perpendicular to magnetic field lines without touching the magnet yoke or balance.
Connects DC supply, variable resistor, ammeter, and switch in series; limits current / switches off between readings to prevent wire overheating.
Measures active magnet length L with a ruler/Vernier callipers and tares balance at I = 0 (or notes untared intercept M₀).
Records balance mass reading across at least six currents (repeating and averaging to reduce random error).
Explains via Newton's 3rd law that an equal opposite downward force acts on the magnet yoke so Δm·g = BIl.
Plots Δm (or M) against I, takes gradient using > 50% span, converts grams to kg, and obtains B = (gradient × 9.81) / L.

parts.prompt: Plan an accurate investigation to verify $F = BIl$ and determine $B$, including circuit wiring, prevention of systematic errors, thermal safety, and how $B$ is extracted even if the balance is untared. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Place the magnet yoke on the 0.01 g balance, clamp the stiff copper rod horizontally and perpendicular to B without touching the yoke, tare the balance at zero current (or record untared intercept M₀), vary current I in six steps with a rheostat while switching off between readings to prevent rod heating; by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current; plot Δm (or M) against I and compute B = (gradient × 9.81) / L using magnet length L.
workingSteps: Level 1: Clamp stiff copper rod horizontally perpendicular to uniform B without touching magnets; series DC supply, rheostat, ammeter, switch.
Level 2: Measure active magnet length L with ruler/callipers; tare balance at I = 0; step current across >= 6 values, opening switch between readings so wire stays cool.
Level 3: Explain N3L downward force on yoke -> Δm g = BIl, plot Δm (or M) vs I, extract B = (gradient × g) / L (converting g to kg).

items.stem: High-power substation transformers step generator output from 11 kV up to 400 kV for national grid transmission.
items.workedSolution: stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared. Transformers rely on continuously changing magnetic flux linkage (Faraday's law), so alternating current is required to step voltage up and down easily. For a given transmitted power P = IV, stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared (P_loss = I²R_line = (P/V)² R_line), dramatically improving grid efficiency. Inside the substation transformer itself, internal energy losses are kept small by: laminating the iron core with thin insulated sheets to raise resistance and suppress eddy-current I²R heating; choosing magnetically soft iron to minimise hysteresis loss during 50 Hz flux reversals; winding coils from thick low-resistivity copper to cut winding I²R losses; and enclosing both coils on a closed overlapping core to prevent magnetic flux leakage.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains AC is required because transformers operate via changing magnetic flux linkage (Faraday's law); DC produces zero steady secondary emf.
L1b: Explains stepping up voltage reduces line current (I = P/V) for fixed power, cutting cable thermal loss P_loss = I²R_line proportionally to 1/V².
L2a: Explains core laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy-current loops, lowering eddy-current I²R core heating.
L2b: Explains magnetically soft iron reduces hysteresis heating during repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation.
L3a: Explains thick low-resistivity copper windings reduce I²R resistive heating in the coils.
L3b: Explains a closed / overlapping iron core ensures almost complete flux linkage between primary and secondary coils (minimising flux leakage).

parts.prompt: Explain why AC and high transmission voltages are essential for efficient national grid power distribution, and explain how the transformer's core and winding construction minimises internal thermal losses.
parts.expectedAnswer: stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared. Transformers rely on continuously changing magnetic flux linkage (Faraday's law), so alternating current is required to step voltage up and down easily. For a given transmitted power P = IV, stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared (P_loss = I²R_line = (P/V)² R_line), dramatically improving grid efficiency. Inside the substation transformer itself, internal energy losses are kept small by: laminating the iron core with thin insulated sheets to raise resistance and suppress eddy-current I²R heating; choosing magnetically soft iron to minimise hysteresis loss during 50 Hz flux reversals; winding coils from thick low-resistivity copper to cut winding I²R losses; and enclosing both coils on a closed overlapping core to prevent magnetic flux leakage.
workingSteps: Justify AC requirement (changing flux needed for mutual induction) and grid step-up via I = P/V and P_loss = I²R.
Explain core eddy-current mitigation (insulated laminations) and hysteresis mitigation (soft iron).
Explain copper winding I²R mitigation (thick low-resistivity copper) and flux-leakage reduction (closed core).

items.stem: When a strong cylindrical magnet falls inside a thick-walled vertical copper tube (g = 9.81 m s⁻²), it quickly reaches a very low constant terminal velocity, whereas an unmagnetised steel cylinder of the same mass accelerates freely.
items.workedSolution: induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy. As the magnet moves inside the conducting copper tube, changing magnetic flux cuts the copper walls and induces circulating eddy currents by Faraday's law (ε ∝ dΦ/dt ∝ v). By Lenz's law, the induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy: eddy currents ahead of the magnet repel its leading pole while eddy currents behind attract its trailing pole, generating an upward braking force proportional to speed v. As speed rises, this upward magnetic drag grows until it balances weight mg, giving zero net force and a slow constant terminal velocity. Throughout steady descent, gravitational potential energy lost converts entirely into I²Rt Joule heating inside the copper pipe rather than kinetic energy; if eddy currents assisted motion, the magnet would gain kinetic and thermal energy simultaneously, violating energy conservation.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Notes copper is non-ferromagnetic but electrically conducting, so falling magnetic flux induces eddy currents in the tube walls (Faraday's law).
L1b: States that by Lenz's law the eddy currents create magnetic fields opposing the magnet's motion (repelling ahead, attracting behind).
L2a: Explains that induced emf, eddy current, and upward magnetic braking force all increase proportionally with speed v.
L2b: States terminal velocity is reached when upward magnetic braking force equals downward weight mg (zero resultant force).
L3a: Accounts for energy: lost gravitational potential energy is transferred via mechanical work against magnetic opposition into I²Rt thermal heating of the copper tube.
L3b: States that if induced eddy currents assisted motion, both kinetic and thermal energy would grow without energy input, violating conservation of energy.

items.stem: During load testing on a laboratory slip-ring alternator with ohmic load, an ideal rotor coil (350 turns, area 0.025 m²) turns at 60 Hz in a uniform 0.3 T field while connected to a 20 Ω resistor. What mean electrical power is dissipated in the resistive load over a complete cycle?
items.workedSolution: Peak emf ε₀ = 2πfNBA = 990 V; V_rms = ε₀ / √2 = 700 V. Mean resistive power P_mean = V_rms² / R = ½ ε₀² / R = 2.45 × 10⁴ W.

markScheme.criterion: Computes ε₀ = 2πfNBA and mean power P_mean = ½ε₀²/R = 2.45 × 10⁴ W (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides peak power V₀I₀ by √2 instead of 2, forgetting that both V_rms = V₀/√2 and I_rms = I₀/√2 contribute a 1/√2 factor.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates peak instantaneous power V₀²/R without applying the ½ sinusoidal average factor.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides V₀ by 2 instead of √2 before squaring in V_rms²/R, introducing a ¼ factor.

items.stem: Ions of two chlorine isotopes carrying charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (m₁ = 5.81 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, m₂ = 6.14 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) emerge from the E = 6.80 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, B₁ = 0.25 T selector of a cosmochemistry meteorite isotope separator into a perpendicular B₂ = 0.6 T deflection chamber (into the page).

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = E / B₁.
Obtains 2.72 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
Uses r₁ = m₁v / (qB₂) with chamber field B₂.
Obtains 0.165 m.
Doubles the radius difference ΔD = 2(r₂ − r₁).
Obtains 0.0187 m.

items.stem: In Required Practical 10, a stiff copper wire of active length $L = 75$ mm sits perpendicularly between slab magnets mounted on a steel yoke atop a 0.01 g digital top-pan balance ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). Plotting balance reading against current $I$ up to 5.0 A produces a straight line of gradient 0.352 g A⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $B = 46.0 mT$. (b) $F = 0.0172 N$. (c) $\Delta m = 1.76 g$. (d) by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current.

markScheme.criterion: Converts gradient to kg A⁻¹ and substitutes into $B = (\mathrm{grad}\cdot g)/L$.
Flux density $B = 46.0 mT$.
Substitutes into $F = B I L$.
Magnetic force $F = 0.0172 N$.
Converts $F/g$ into grams.
Mass change $\Delta m = 1.76 g$.
States magnetic field exerts an upward force on the clamped wire.
Applies Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite downward force on magnet yoke raises balance reading.

parts.prompt: Use the gradient to calculate the magnetic flux density $B$ in mT.
Calculate the magnetic force on the wire at the maximum current of 5.0 A.
Calculate the change in balance reading $\Delta m$ (in g) at this maximum current.
Explain using Newton's third law why the balance reading changes even though the wire is clamped independently.
parts.expectedAnswer: by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current
workingSteps: Magnetic field exerts an upward force BIl on the current-carrying wire.
By Newton's 3rd law, the wire exerts an equal downward force BIl on the magnets/yoke, increasing the balance normal reaction.

items.stem: Perpendicular magnetic field lines through a closed earth-inductor compass loop (75 turns, area 0.022 m², resistance 2 Ω) change from +0.35 T to −0.350 T in 0.2 s. What total magnitude of electric charge ΔQ flows around the circuit during this reversal?
items.workedSolution: Signed field change |ΔB| = |-0.35 − 0.35| = 0.7 T, so |Δ(NΦ)| = 75 × 0.7 × 0.022 = 1.15 Wb. Induced charge ΔQ = |Δ(NΦ)| / R = 0.577 C.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for field sign reversal in |Δ(NΦ)| and evaluates ΔQ = |Δ(NΦ)|/R = 0.577 C (A).

items.stem: Travelling to the left at constant velocity 8 m s⁻¹, a crossbar of resistance 0.4 Ω spans frictionless rails 0.2 m apart on a linear regenerator test track connected to a 1.4 Ω load in a 0.9 T field (directed out of the page). What induced current circulates around the closed loop?
items.workedSolution: Motional emf ε = BLv = 0.9 × 0.2 × 8 = 1.44 V. Loop current I = ε / (R + r) = 1.44 / 1.8 = 0.800 A.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I = BLv / (R + r) = 0.800 A (B).

items.stem: In the student switched RC bench rig shown, a capacitor of capacitance C = 200 μF is first fully charged to V₀ = 8.00 V by closing Switch A while Switches B and C remain open. Switch A is then opened and Switch B is closed so the capacitor discharges through R₁ = 90 kΩ for 12.0 s. At t = 12.0 s, while Switch B stays closed, Switch C is closed to connect R₂ = 45 kΩ in parallel with R₁ for a further 6.00 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b)(i) τ₁ = R₁C = 18.00 s, so V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁) = 4.107 V ≈ 4.11 V (confirming 4.1 V). (b)(ii) R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 30.0 kΩ, giving τ₂ = R_eq C = 6.000 s ≈ 6.00 s. (b)(iii) V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂) = 1.511 V ≈ 1.51 V. (b)(iv) smaller final potential difference because the time constant decreases and the capacitor discharges more rapidly.

markScheme.criterion: Mentions charge stored per unit potential difference (coulombs per volt).
Complete SI unit definition: capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Evaluates stage-1 time constant τ₁ = R₁C = 18.0 s.
Correctly substitutes V₀, t₁, and τ₁ into V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁).
Shows V₁ = 4.107 V (≥3 s.f.: 4.11 V), clearly matching 4.1 V.
Combines R₁ || R₂ = 30.0 kΩ and calculates τ₂ = R_eq C = 6.00 s.
Substitutes V₁ (accepting rounded prompt value on ECF), t₂, and τ₂ into V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂).
Correct final potential difference V₂ = 1.51 V.
States correctly that V₂ would be smaller (smaller/larger matching direction).
Explains via time constants in both stages: smaller final potential difference because the time constant decreases and the capacitor discharges more rapidly.
