parts.prompt: Define the farad.
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the unit definition linking electric charge in coulombs and potential difference in volts.

parts.prompt: Show clearly that after discharging through R₁ alone for 12.0 s, the potential difference across the capacitor is approximately 4.1 V.
parts.expectedAnswer: 4.107 V (which rounds to 4.11 V and 4.1 V)
workingSteps: Stage 1 time constant τ₁ = R₁ C = (90 × 10³ Ω) × (200 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 18.00 s.
Substitute into V₁ = V₀ exp(−t₁ / τ₁) = 8.000 V × exp(−12 / 18.00 s).
Evaluate to 4 s.f.: V₁ = 4.107 V ≈ 4.11 V (confirming approximately 4.1 V).

parts.prompt: At the instant Switch C closes, calculate the new time constant τ₂ of the discharge circuit.
workingSteps: Combined parallel resistance R_eq = (R₁ R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (90 × 45) / (90 + 45) = 30.0 kΩ.
New time constant τ₂ = R_eq C = (30 × 10³ Ω) × (200 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 6.000 s ≈ 6.00 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference V₂ across the capacitor after a further 6.00 s with both Switch B and Switch C closed.
workingSteps: Start Stage 2 decay from V₁ = 4.107 V with time constant τ₂ = 6.000 s.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how the final potential difference V₂ would change if resistor R₁ were replaced by a smaller resistor throughout the entire experiment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing the first resistor with a smaller resistor gives a smaller final potential difference because the time constant decreases and the capacitor discharges more rapidly.
workingSteps: A smaller resistance changes both the initial discharge time constant and the combined parallel resistance in the same direction.
Link the altered time constants in both stages to the rate of exponential decay and the remaining potential difference.

items.stem: After disconnecting its charging cell in a pulsed laser pre-ioniser loop, capacitor C₁ = 20 μF at V₁ = 17 V shares charge across switch S with C₂ = 60 μF, which is initially uncharged. How much electrostatic energy is dissipated in the connecting leads as equilibrium is reached?
items.workedSolution: Initial energy U_i = 2.89 × 10⁻³ J. Final common voltage V_f = 4.25 V gives final energy U_f = ½(C₁ + C₂)V_f² = 7.22 × 10⁻⁴ J. Energy dissipated ΔU = U_i − U_f = 2.17 × 10⁻³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates U_i − U_f after conserving charge to obtain 2.17 × 10⁻³ J (D).

items.workedSolution: Because precession frequency depends on local $B$, gradient field coils vary magnetic flux density across the patient to scan successive small regions.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that gradient field coils vary magnetic flux density across the patient to scan successive small regions.

items.stem: Fixed so that a uniform magnetic field forms an angle of 25° with the plane of the coil, a closed search coil in an MRI fringe-field survey of 60 turns, area 0.016 m², and resistance 5 Ω experiences a field that decays uniformly from 0.56 T to zero in 0.1 s. What average induced current circulates around the closed coil during the ramp?
items.workedSolution: With θ_normal = 65°, |ε| = N|ΔB|A cos 65° / Δt = 2.27 V. Average current I = |ε| / R = 2.27 / 5 = 0.454 A.

markScheme.criterion: Computes |ε| using θ_normal = 65° and I = |ε|/R = 0.454 A (B).

markScheme.criterion: Finds initial C = εᵣε₀A/d and applies U_i = ½CV².

items.stem: In a camera strobe flash bank, two initially uncharged capacitors of capacitances C₁ = 12 μF and C₂ = 24 μF are connected in series across a 11 V DC source. What is the total equivalent capacitance of the series pair?
items.workedSolution: For series capacitors, 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂, giving C_eq = (12 × 24)/(12 + 24) μF = 8.00 × 10⁻⁶ F.

markScheme.criterion: Uses 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ to obtain 8.00 × 10⁻⁶ F (B).

items.stem: Physicists inspect a bubble-chamber photograph taken in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page showing a pair-creation event.
items.workedSolution: With magnetic field into the page a rightward positron curves upwards while a rightward electron curves downwards by Fleming left-hand rule. Neutral photons cannot ionise liquid hydrogen directly, so no track precedes the vertex. Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with B into the page shows opposite curvature identifies opposite charges: rightward positrons deflect upwards while rightward electrons deflect downwards. Measuring initial curvature radius r determines momentum via p = BQr. Ionising collisions transfer kinetic energy to liquid hydrogen, reducing momentum p and shrinking radius r into inward spirals.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Explains neutral particles (such as gamma photons) do not ionise liquid hydrogen and therefore leave no track.
L1: States charged particles create trails of vapour bubbles by ionising liquid hydrogen along their paths.
L2: Uses Fleming's left-hand rule with B into the page to link opposite deflection directions to opposite charges (e⁺ up, e⁻ down).
L2: Equates magnetic centripetal force BQv = mv²/r to obtain r = p/(BQ) for calculating momentum.
L3: Explains that equal initial radii imply equal initial magnitudes of momentum for the created e⁻/e⁺ pair.
L3: Explains inward spiralling is caused by continuous kinetic energy and momentum loss via ionising collisions.

parts.prompt: Explain how physicists deduce (i) that the incident particle was neutral, (ii) the sign of each created particle's charge, (iii) each particle's initial momentum, and (iv) why both tracks spiral inwards. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: With magnetic field into the page a rightward positron curves upwards while a rightward electron curves downwards by Fleming left-hand rule. Neutral photons cannot ionise liquid hydrogen directly, so no track precedes the vertex. Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with B into the page shows opposite curvature identifies opposite charges: rightward positrons deflect upwards while rightward electrons deflect downwards. Measuring initial curvature radius r determines momentum via p = BQr. Ionising collisions transfer kinetic energy to liquid hydrogen, reducing momentum p and shrinking radius r into inward spirals.
workingSteps: Explain why neutral particles leave no ionisation track before the pair-production vertex.
Apply Fleming's left-hand rule with B into the page to identify e⁺ (curving up) vs e⁻ (curving down).
Use r = p/(BQ) for initial momentum and link ionisation energy loss to decreasing radius (inward spiral).

items.stem: In an accelerator monochromatic ion collimator, parallel plates separated by 0.02 m are held at 240 V (upper plate negative) perpendicular to a uniform 0.2 T magnetic field (out of the page). A proton (charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is injected horizontally to the right at 3.60 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E = V / d.
Obtains 1.20 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.
Equates qE = qvB to obtain v_sel = E / B.
Obtains 6.00 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.
Uses a_y = q(E − vB) / m.
Obtains 4.60 × 10¹¹ m s⁻².

workingSteps: Parallel branch: C_p = C₂ + C₃ = 120 + 105 = 225 μF.

parts.prompt: Determine the maximum safe potential difference that can be applied across A and B, stating which section reaches its voltage rating first.
parts.expectedAnswer: 133 V (limited by the single series capacitor)
workingSteps: In series both sections hold equal charge Q, so V ∝ 1/C; the smaller capacitance (single series capacitor) reaches 100 V first.
Maximum safe total pd V_AB,max = 100 × (1 + 75 / 225) = 133.3 V ≈ 133 V.

items.stem: A search coil with $N = 1500$ turns of cross-sectional area 2.0 cm² sits at angle $\theta = 48^\circ$ (between normal and field) inside a 60 Hz alternating magnetic field of peak flux density 3.2 mT (RP11). Calculate the peak-to-peak voltage $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ displayed on the CRO.
items.workedSolution: Peak induced emf $\varepsilon_0 = 2\pi f B A N \cos\theta$ and $V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 2\varepsilon_0 = (4\pi f B A N)\cos\theta$. Substituting $A = 2\times 10^{-4}$ m² gives gradient $= 724 mV$, $B = 3.2$ mT, $\varepsilon_0 = 242 mV$, and $V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 484 mV$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines vPeakToPeakMv $= 484 mV$.

items.stem: A power station upgrades its step-up transformer to triple the overhead transmission voltage while delivering the same total electrical power along the same cables. Why do resistive cable losses drop by a factor of nine?
items.workedSolution: Since I = P/V and P_loss = I²R, stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared. Therefore the correct statement is: Because stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: stepping up transmission voltage lowers cable current for the same power so resistive heating in power lines falls as current squared.

items.stem: At the instant a falling bar magnet passes the exact centre of a solenoid, the induced emf briefly reads zero before reversing polarity. Why is the emf zero at the centre even though magnetic flux linkage is at its maximum, and how do the two pulses compare?
items.workedSolution: At maximum flux linkage its rate of change is zero, and the exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage. Therefore the correct statement is: At the centre dΦ/dt is instantaneously zero, and overall the exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage.

options.text: At the centre dΦ/dt is instantaneously zero, and overall the exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage

options.label: B
options.text: At the centre magnetic flux drops to zero, so the exit pulse has half the enclosed area of the entry pulse.
options.distractorRationale: Flux is maximal (not zero) at the centre, and both pulses have equal enclosed area NΦ.

options.label: C
options.text: At the centre the magnet momentarily stops moving under Lenz repulsion, making both pulses symmetric.
options.distractorRationale: The magnet continues falling and accelerating, making the exit pulse taller and narrower.

options.label: D
options.text: At the centre Faraday's law depends on total flux rather than rate of change of flux, so exit area exceeds entry area.
options.distractorRationale: Faraday's law depends on rate of change of flux linkage N dΦ/dt, whose time integral equals NΦ for both halves.

items.stem: An industrial testing facility uses a 92.0% efficient step-up transformer fed at 230 V and connects a high-voltage feeder line of resistance 8.00 Ω. The transformer has Nₚ = 500 primary turns, Nₛ = 2500 secondary turns, and primary voltage Vₚ = 230 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vₛ = 1.15 × 10³ V. (b) Iₚ = 24.5 A. (c) P_loss = 8.00 × 10⁶ W. (d) thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates Vₛ = 1.15 × 10³ V.
Applies η = (Iₛ Vₛ) / (Iₚ Vₚ).
Obtains Iₚ = 24.5 A.
Finds cable current I = P / Vₛ = 1.00 × 10³ A.
Calculates cable loss P_loss = I²R = 8.00 × 10⁶ W.
States insulating layers between iron sheets increase resistance to eddy currents.
Links smaller eddy currents to reduced I²R core heating (thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core).

items.stem: A benchtop AC power pack supplies a 40.0 Ω immersion element monitored with a cathode-ray oscilloscope. The oscilloscope is set to Y-gain 5.00 V div⁻¹ and time-base 2.00 ms div⁻¹. The sinusoidal trace spans 5.00 divisions peak-to-peak and 5.00 horizontal divisions per complete cycle.
items.workedSolution: (a) V_rms = 8.84 V. (b) f = 100 Hz. (c) P_mean = 1.95 W. (d) switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Finds peak voltage V₀ = 12.5 V by halving peak-to-peak height.
Divides by √2 to obtain V_rms = 8.84 V.
Calculates period T = 0.0100 s.
Inverts T to obtain f = 100 Hz.
Evaluates P_mean = V_rms² / R = 1.95 W.
States horizontal deflection ceases so spot oscillates vertically at the centre.
States full length equals peak-to-peak voltage (switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage).

parts.prompt: Calculate the root-mean-square potential difference V_rms across the resistor.
Determine the frequency f of the alternating supply.
Calculate the mean power dissipated in the load resistor.
Describe and explain what appears on the oscilloscope screen if the time-base is switched OFF.

items.stem: During thermal-loss testing of a rack-mounted server isolation-stepdown unit, a 120 V rms primary supply energises 800 primary turns coupled to 40 secondary turns across a 24 Ω load with efficiency η = 0.88 (88%). What rms current is drawn from the primary AC supply?
items.workedSolution: Secondary rms voltage V_s = V_p(N_s/N_p) = 120(40/800) = 6.00 V. Output power P_out = V_s² / R_L = 1.50 W. Input power P_in = P_out / η = 1.70 W, so I_p = P_in / V_p = 0.0142 A.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V_s, P_out, and I_p = P_out / (η V_p) = 0.0142 A (D).

items.stem: Connected via slip rings to a 80 Ω load in a marine diesel-electric AC load-testing unit, an ideal coil of 220 turns and area 0.012 m² rotates at 80 Hz in a uniform 0.48 T magnetic field.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε₀ = 2πfNBA.
Obtains 637 V.
Uses I_rms = ε₀ / (√2 R).
Obtains 5.63 A.
Applies P_mean = I_rms² R (= ½ ε₀ I₀).
Obtains 2.54 × 10³ W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak emf ε₀ induced in the rotating coil.
Determine the rms current in the resistive load.
Calculate the mean electrical power dissipated in the load.

items.stem: Selected at common speed by E = 4.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B₁ = 0.25 T in a paleoclimate ice-core Bainbridge analyser, chlorine ions of charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and masses m₁ = 5.81 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and m₂ = 6.14 × 10⁻²⁶ kg enter a uniform B₂ = 0.6 T chamber (into the page) and complete semicircular paths. What is the straight-line separation ΔD between the two isotope strike marks on the detector wall?
items.workedSolution: Selected speed v = E / B₁ = 1.60 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Semicircular strike separation ΔD = 2(r₂ − r₁) = 2(m₂ − m₁)E / (q B₁ B₂) = 0.0110 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ΔD = 2|m₂ − m₁|E / (qB₁B₂) = 0.0110 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the difference in orbital radii |r₂ − r₁| and forgets the factor of 2 for semicircular impact diameters ΔD = 2|r₂ − r₁|.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses B₁² in the denominator instead of the product B₁B₂ of selector and chamber fields.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports the semicircular strike distance 2r₁ of the lighter isotope rather than the separation between isotopes.

items.stem: During Required Practical 10, slab magnets with uniform flux density $B = 72$ mT span an active wire length $L = 50$ mm ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). What is the expected gradient of the top-pan balance reading $M$ (in g) plotted against current $I$ (in A)?
items.workedSolution: Using $\Delta m \cdot g = B I L$ with $g = 9.81$ m s⁻², gradient $= 1000 B L / g = 0.367 g A⁻¹$, $B = 72$ mT, $F = B I L = 0.0144 N$, and untared reading $= 168.4 + 1.47 = 169.9 g$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines gradMvsI_gPerA $= 0.367 g A⁻¹$.

items.stem: Aligned normal to the axis of an electromagnet, an earth-inductor compass loop (500 turns, area 0.022 m², loop resistance 2 Ω) experiences a polarity reversal from +0.18 T to −0.180 T over 0.2 s.

markScheme.criterion: Includes negative sign of reversed field in N(B₂ − B₁)A.
Obtains −3.96 Wb.
Divides |Δ(NΦ)| from (a) by Δt.
Obtains 19.8 V.
Uses ΔQ = |Δ(NΦ)| / R (or I_avg Δt).
Obtains 1.98 C.

items.stem: In the electronic shutter decay bank shown, a capacitor of capacitance C = 220 μF is first fully charged to V₀ = 11.0 V by closing Switch A while Switches B and C remain open. Switch A is then opened and Switch B is closed so the capacitor discharges through R₁ = 60 kΩ for 9.00 s. At t = 9.00 s, while Switch B stays closed, Switch C is closed to connect R₂ = 20 kΩ in parallel with R₁ for a further 4.00 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b)(i) τ₁ = R₁C = 13.20 s, so V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁) = 5.563 V ≈ 5.56 V (confirming 5.6 V). (b)(ii) R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 15.0 kΩ, giving τ₂ = R_eq C = 3.300 s ≈ 3.30 s. (b)(iii) V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂) = 1.655 V ≈ 1.66 V. (b)(iv) smaller final potential difference because the time constant decreases and the capacitor discharges more rapidly.

markScheme.criterion: Mentions charge stored per unit potential difference (coulombs per volt).
Complete SI unit definition: capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Evaluates stage-1 time constant τ₁ = R₁C = 13.2 s.
Correctly substitutes V₀, t₁, and τ₁ into V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁).
Shows V₁ = 5.563 V (≥3 s.f.: 5.56 V), clearly matching 5.6 V.
Combines R₁ || R₂ = 15.0 kΩ and calculates τ₂ = R_eq C = 3.30 s.
Substitutes V₁ (accepting rounded prompt value on ECF), t₂, and τ₂ into V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂).
Correct final potential difference V₂ = 1.66 V.
States correctly that V₂ would be smaller (smaller/larger matching direction).
Explains via time constants in both stages: smaller final potential difference because the time constant decreases and the capacitor discharges more rapidly.

parts.prompt: Define the farad.
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the unit definition linking electric charge in coulombs and potential difference in volts.

parts.prompt: Show clearly that after discharging through R₁ alone for 9.00 s, the potential difference across the capacitor is approximately 5.6 V.
parts.expectedAnswer: 5.563 V (which rounds to 5.56 V and 5.6 V)
workingSteps: Stage 1 time constant τ₁ = R₁ C = (60 × 10³ Ω) × (220 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 13.20 s.
Substitute into V₁ = V₀ exp(−t₁ / τ₁) = 11.00 V × exp(−9 / 13.20 s).
Evaluate to 4 s.f.: V₁ = 5.563 V ≈ 5.56 V (confirming approximately 5.6 V).

parts.prompt: At the instant Switch C closes, calculate the new time constant τ₂ of the discharge circuit.
workingSteps: Combined parallel resistance R_eq = (R₁ R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (60 × 20) / (60 + 20) = 15.0 kΩ.
New time constant τ₂ = R_eq C = (15 × 10³ Ω) × (220 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 3.300 s ≈ 3.30 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference V₂ across the capacitor after a further 4.00 s with both Switch B and Switch C closed.
workingSteps: Start Stage 2 decay from V₁ = 5.563 V with time constant τ₂ = 3.300 s.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how the final potential difference V₂ would change if resistor R₁ were replaced by a smaller resistor throughout the entire experiment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing the first resistor with a smaller resistor gives a smaller final potential difference because the time constant decreases and the capacitor discharges more rapidly.
workingSteps: A smaller resistance changes both the initial discharge time constant and the combined parallel resistance in the same direction.
Link the altered time constants in both stages to the rate of exponential decay and the remaining potential difference.

Divides conserved charge from (a) by C₁ + C₂.
Obtains 7.40 V.
Subtracts final stored energy ½(C₁ + C₂)V_f² from initial stored energy.
Obtains 0.0110 J.

items.stem: In a Thomson crossed-field velocity selector, a horizontal electron beam passes undeflected between parallel plates separated by 4.00 cm with a potential difference of 1080 V across them, in a perpendicular uniform magnetic flux density of 1.50 mT. What is the speed of the electrons?
items.workedSolution: For zero net deflection, $eE = Bev$, so $v = \frac{E}{B} = \frac{V_p}{Bd} = \frac{1080}{1.50 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.0400} = 1.80 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.80 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: To characterise polystyrene slab of relative permittivity 6, a radio-frequency tuning plate assembly with plate area 0.9 m² and plate spacing 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m is energised by a 320 V DC source (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹). calculate the capacitance of the dielectric-filled assembly.

markScheme.criterion: Applies C = εᵣε₀A / d to obtain 7.97 × 10⁻⁸ F (C).

items.stem: An experimental rotary position-sensing pickup winding comprises 300 closely wound turns of area 0.016 m² and resistance 5 Ω. Held at a fixed orientation where the field lines make an angle of 35° with the plane of the coil, the field ramps uniformly from 0.36 T to 1.08 T over 0.05 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses θ_normal = 55° in NΦ₁ = NBA cos θ_normal.
Obtains 0.991 Wb.
Applies Faraday's law |ε| = |NΦ₂ − NΦ₁| / Δt.
Obtains 39.6 V.
Divides induced emf from (b) by coil resistance R.
Obtains 7.93 A.

items.stem: Emerging through the anode aperture after acceleration from rest across 3600 V in a surface-science low-energy ion scattering rig, a doubly ionised magnesium ion (+3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 3.98 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) enters at 90° to a homogeneous 0.320 T magnetic field (out of the page). If the particle completes a semicircular turn onto an exit detector plate, what is the strike diameter D from the entry slit?
items.workedSolution: Speed v = √(2|q|V_acc / m) = 2.41 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; radius r = mv / (|q|B) = 0.0935 m. Semicircular detector separation D = 2r = 0.187 m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes D = (2/B)√(2mV_acc / |q|) = 0.187 m (D).

items.stem: A piezo-positioned capacitor stage has plate area 0.25 m², initial separation 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m, and relative permittivity 4, energised initially at 100 V (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹). Next, the assembly is kept connected across the DC source at constant potential difference while the plate separation is adjusted to 0.001 m with εᵣ = 4 throughout. What is the final electrostatic energy stored in the modified state?
items.workedSolution: Initial capacitance C = 2.21 × 10⁻⁸ F, modified capacitance C′ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁹ F. Under constant-voltage, final stored energy U′ = 4.42 × 10⁻⁵ J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes modified capacitance C′ and evaluates final stored energy 4.42 × 10⁻⁵ J (D).

items.stem: In a biomedical amplifier coupling network, parallel branches containing C_p1 = 10 μF and C_p2 = 20 μF are wired in series with capacitor C_s = 30 μF and charged by a steady 7 V source.

markScheme.criterion: Sums C_p = C_p1 + C_p2 and combines in series with C_s.
Obtains 1.50 × 10⁻⁵ F.
Finds total charge Q = C_eq V₀ and divides by C_p.
Obtains 3.50 V.
Evaluates U = ½C_eq V₀².
Obtains 3.67 × 10⁻⁴ J.

items.stem: Inside a fine-beam Helmholtz tube, an electron (charge −1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) enters at 8.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform 2.40 × 10⁻³ T magnetic field directed into the page and follows a circular arc. What is the radius of curvature r of the circular path?
items.workedSolution: Equating magnetic and centripetal forces |q|vB = mv²/r gives r = mv / (|q|B) = (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 8.00 × 10⁶) / (0 × 2.40 × 10⁻³) = 0.0190 m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates r = mv / (|q|B) = 0.0190 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the cyclotron radius formula and evaluates |q|B / (mv) instead of mv / (|q|B).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Confuses orbital radius r = mv/(|q|B) with semicircular orbit diameter D = 2r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses mv²/(|q|B) by forgetting to cancel one power of speed v when equating mv²/r = |q|vB.

items.stem: Why does a proton travelling along the central axis of a linac experience acceleration only between adjacent drift tubes and not while passing through the interior of a tube?
items.workedSolution: Hollow metallic drift tubes act as Faraday cages with zero internal electric field, shielding particles while the RF polarity reverses. Therefore the correct statement is: Because inside each hollow conducting drift tube the electric field is zero so particles move at constant speed and accelerate only across the gaps.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: inside each hollow conducting drift tube the electric field is zero so particles move at constant speed and accelerate only across the gaps.

options.label: A
options.text: Because a strong transverse magnetic field inside each tube cancels the forward electric force.
options.distractorRationale: Linac drift tubes rely on electrostatic shielding, not cancelling magnetic fields.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the AC supply is switched off completely whenever protons enter a drift tube.
options.distractorRationale: The AC voltage reverses polarity smoothly while the beam is shielded inside the tube.

options.label: C
options.text: Because inside each hollow conducting drift tube the electric field is zero so particles move at constant speed and accelerate only across the gaps.

options.label: D
options.text: Because protons become electrically neutral inside a metal cylinder and regain charge in the vacuum gaps.
options.distractorRationale: Proton charge +e is invariant; the interior electric field is zero inside a Faraday-shielded conductor.

items.stem: During tuning of an accelerator-mass-spectrometry pre-filter (180 V across a 0.03 m gap, upper plate positive, with B = 0.32 T into the page), a proton of charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg is injected horizontally along the central axis. At what speed must the proton travel to pass straight through the exit slit undeflected?
items.workedSolution: Uniform electric field E = V / d = 180 / 0.03 = 6.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹. Zero net deflection requires qE = qvB, so v_sel = E / B = V / (Bd) = 1.88 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_sel = V / (Bd) to obtain 1.88 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: In the power-supply smoothing stage shown between terminals A and B, capacitor C₁ = 60 μF is connected in series with the parallel pair C₂ = 80 μF and C₃ = 40 μF. Every capacitor has a maximum safe working voltage of 50 V. What is the maximum safe potential difference that can be applied across terminals A and B without exceeding the rating of any capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel pair C_p = C₂ + C₃ = 120 μF. Because C₁ (60 μF) and C_p (120 μF) carry equal series charge Q, the smaller capacitance (single series capacitor) reaches 50 V first. Thus V_AB,max = 50 × (1 + 60 / 120) = 75.00 V ≈ 75.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the single series capacitor limits the voltage and calculates V_AB,max = 75.0 V.

items.stem: In Required Practical 11, a search coil with $N = 2000$ turns of area 1.5 cm² is centred inside a large circular coil driven by a 50 Hz AC supply. With the CRO Y-gain set to 100 mV div⁻¹ and the coil normal at $\theta = 35^\circ$ to the field, the peak-to-peak vertical trace spans 6.49 divisions.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 649 mV$. (b) Gradient $= 792 mV$. (c) $B = 4.20 mT$. (d) a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies peak-to-peak divisions by Y-gain.
$V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 649 mV$.
Divides $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ by $\cos 35^\circ$.
Gradient $= 792 mV$.
Applies $V_{\mathrm{pp,max}} = 4\pi f B A N$ with $A$ in m².
Peak flux density $B = 4.20 mT$.
Static DC field gives zero rate of change of flux linkage, so zero induced emf.
Use a Hall probe to measure static DC magnetic flux density.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak-to-peak induced voltage $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ at $\theta = 35^\circ$.
Hence calculate the gradient of the straight-line graph of $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ against $\cos\theta$.
Use $\varepsilon_0 = 2\pi f B A N$ to determine the peak magnetic flux density $B$ in mT.
workingSteps: Gradient $= 4\pi f B A N$, so $B = (792\times 10^{-3}) / (4\pi \times 50 \times 1.5\times 10^{-4} \times 2000) = 4.20 mT$.

parts.prompt: Explain why the search coil fails if the AC supply is replaced by a DC battery, and state what sensor should be used instead.
parts.expectedAnswer: a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density
workingSteps: Faraday's law requires rate of change of flux linkage d(NΦ)/dt ≠ 0, which is zero in static DC.
Use a calibrated Hall probe (perpendicular to field) for static DC flux density.

items.stem: Within an industrial watchdog reset timer, a 24 V DC rail charges an initially uncharged 25 μF capacitor via a 2.5 kΩ series resistor; the transient is evaluated at 0.138 s.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies resistance in Ω by capacitance in F (τ = RC).
Obtains 0.0625 s.
Applies V_C(t) = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)).
Obtains 21.4 V.
Uses U = ½CV_C² with the voltage found in (b).
Obtains 5.70 × 10⁻³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the RC time constant τ of the circuit.
Determine the potential difference across the capacitor at t = 0.138 s.
Calculate the electrostatic energy stored in the capacitor at t = 0.138 s.

items.stem: Driven at a rotational frequency of 40 Hz inside a wind-tunnel slip-ring test dynamo, a slip-ring coil of 50 turns and area 0.03 m² cuts a uniform 0.14 T magnetic field (starting from maximum flux at t = 0 and observed at t = 0.00208 s). What is the peak-to-peak emf displayed on an oscilloscope across one full cycle?
items.workedSolution: Peak emf ε₀ = 2πfNBA = 52.8 V. Peak-to-peak emf V_pp = 2ε₀ = 106 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V_pp = 2(2πfNBA) = 106 V (B).

options.distractorRationale: Computes rms voltage ε₀/√2 instead of peak-to-peak voltage 2ε₀.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 2 for peak-to-peak but omits 2π when converting f to ω.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Reports single-sided peak amplitude ε₀ rather than peak-to-peak swing 2ε₀.

items.stem: Travelling at an initial horizontal speed of 5.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, a proton (q = +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) passes centrally between parallel plates of length 0.05 m spaced 0.04 m apart across a 1140 V potential difference in an inkjet micro-droplet deflection stage. What is the angular deflection θ (in degrees) of the particle velocity as it leaves the plates?
items.workedSolution: |v_y| = a_y t = (|q|V / md)(L / v₀) = 2.73 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Therefore θ = arctan(|v_y| / v₀) = 28.6°.

markScheme.criterion: Finds |v_y| and evaluates θ = arctan(|v_y|/v₀) = 28.6° (D).

items.stem: A medical cyclotron uses a uniform magnetic flux density B = 1.50 T and hollow metal dees of maximum radius R = 0.40 m to accelerate protons (m = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, Q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.workedSolution: (a) 22.8 MHz. (b) 5.74 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (c) 17.2 MeV. (d) one tesla is the magnetic flux density that exerts a force of one newton per metre on a wire carrying a current of one ampere perpendicular to the magnetic field.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f = BQ / (2πm).
Obtains f = 22.8 MHz.
Rearranges BQv = mv²/R to v = BQR/m.
Obtains v = 5.74 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
Computes exit KE = 17.2 MeV.
Defines 1 T via 1 N per metre on a 1 A wire.
Explicitly specifies the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field.

items.stem: Ten narrow cycles of an AC signal crowd onto an oscilloscope screen. How should a student adjust the time-base setting to measure the period T more precisely?
items.workedSolution: Decreasing the time-base setting stretches the waveform horizontally so fewer cycles span the screen and percentage uncertainty in period decreases. Therefore the correct statement is: Adjust the dial carefully because decreasing the time-base setting stretches the waveform horizontally so fewer cycles span the screen and percentage uncertainty in period decreases

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: decreasing the time-base setting stretches the waveform horizontally so fewer cycles span the screen and percentage uncertainty in period decreases.

options.label: A
options.text: Adjust the dial carefully because increasing the time-base setting stretches a single cycle across the entire width of the screen.
options.distractorRationale: Increasing ms div⁻¹ compresses more cycles per division rather than stretching one cycle.

options.label: B
options.text: Adjust the dial carefully because decreasing the time-base setting stretches the waveform horizontally so fewer cycles span the screen and percentage uncertainty in period decreases

options.label: C
options.text: Adjust the dial carefully because switching off the time base lets you read the period directly off the vertical axis.
options.distractorRationale: Time-base OFF removes all time/frequency information from the display.

options.label: D
options.text: Adjust the dial carefully because decreasing the Y-gain stretches the horizontal time axis across more divisions.
options.distractorRationale: Y-gain only scales vertical voltage amplitude, not horizontal time.

markScheme.criterion: Applies η = IₛVₛ / (IₚVₚ) to obtain Iₚ = 16.3 A.

items.stem: A bar magnet is dropped from rest above a solenoid wired to a data logger, producing two opposite-polarity emf pulses as it enters and leaves. How do the height, width, and enclosed area of the exit pulse compare with the entry pulse?
items.workedSolution: Since ε = −N dΦ/dt and ∫|ε| dt = NΔΦ, the exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage. Therefore the correct statement is: The exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: exit pulse has greater peak emf and shorter duration because the magnet accelerates under gravity while both pulses enclose equal area equal to maximum flux linkage.

items.stem: A university solar microgrid boosts 400 V inverter output using a 94.0% efficient laminated-core transformer connected to a 5.00 Ω campus cable. The transformer has Nₚ = 800 primary turns, Nₛ = 4000 secondary turns, and primary voltage Vₚ = 400 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vₛ = 2.00 × 10³ V. (b) Iₚ = 31.9 A. (c) P_loss = 3.20 × 10⁶ W. (d) thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates Vₛ = 2.00 × 10³ V.
Applies η = (Iₛ Vₛ) / (Iₚ Vₚ).
Obtains Iₚ = 31.9 A.
Finds cable current I = P / Vₛ = 800 A.
Calculates cable loss P_loss = I²R = 3.20 × 10⁶ W.
States insulating layers between iron sheets increase resistance to eddy currents.
Links smaller eddy currents to reduced I²R core heating (thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core).

If power 1.60 × 10⁶ W is transmitted at voltage Vₛ along cables of total resistance 5.00 Ω, calculate the thermal power dissipated in the cables.
Explain how laminating the soft-iron core reduces internal thermal energy losses in the transformer.
parts.expectedAnswer: Laminating the core works because thin iron laminations separated by insulating layers increase resistance to eddy current paths reducing thermal energy loss in the core.

items.stem: An audio signal generator drives a 25.0 Ω loudspeaker load while monitored on a calibrated 10 × 8 division oscilloscope. The oscilloscope is set to Y-gain 2.00 V div⁻¹ and time-base 5.00 ms div⁻¹. The sinusoidal trace spans 6.00 divisions peak-to-peak and 4.00 horizontal divisions per complete cycle.
items.workedSolution: (a) V_rms = 4.24 V. (b) f = 50.0 Hz. (c) P_mean = 0.720 W. (d) switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Finds peak voltage V₀ = 6.00 V by halving peak-to-peak height.
Divides by √2 to obtain V_rms = 4.24 V.
Calculates period T = 0.0200 s.
Inverts T to obtain f = 50.0 Hz.
Evaluates P_mean = V_rms² / R = 0.720 W.
States horizontal deflection ceases so spot oscillates vertically at the centre.
States full length equals peak-to-peak voltage (switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage).

parts.prompt: Calculate the root-mean-square potential difference V_rms across the resistor.

Describe and explain what appears on the oscilloscope screen if the time-base is switched OFF.
parts.expectedAnswer: With no horizontal sweep, switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.
workingSteps: Without horizontal deflection the electron beam moves purely vertically between +V₀ and −V₀.
switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

items.stem: A micro-grid synchronous generator bench uses a coil of negligible internal resistance with 180 turns and area 0.025 m² spinning at 25 Hz in a uniform 0.22 T magnetic field across a 16 Ω resistor. What root-mean-square (rms) current flows through the load resistor?
items.workedSolution: ε₀ = 2πfNBA = 156 V, so V_rms = ε₀ / √2 = 110 V. Load rms current I_rms = V_rms / R = 110 / 16 = 6.87 A.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I_rms = 2πfNBA / (√2 R) = 6.87 A (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 2π factor when converting frequency f into angular speed ω = 2πf.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates peak current I₀ = ε₀/R and omits dividing by √2 for rms current.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides peak current I₀ by 2 instead of √2.

items.stem: Operating with selector electric field 6.80 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, selector flux density 0.35 T, and chamber flux density 0.7 T (out of the page), a planetary-probe isotopic magnetic sector separates carbon ions of charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and masses 1.99 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and 2.32 × 10⁻²⁶ kg onto a flat detector plane.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = E / B₁.
Obtains 1.94 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
Uses r₁ = m₁v / (qB₂) with chamber field B₂.
Obtains 0.0345 m.
Doubles the radius difference ΔD = 2(r₂ − r₁).
Obtains 0.0114 m.

items.stem: In Required Practical 10, a stiff copper wire of active length $L = 45$ mm sits perpendicularly between slab magnets mounted on a steel yoke atop a 0.01 g digital top-pan balance ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). Plotting balance reading against current $I$ up to 3.6 A produces a straight line of gradient 0.385 g A⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $B = 84.0 mT$. (b) $F = 0.0136 N$. (c) $\Delta m = 1.39 g$. (d) by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current.

markScheme.criterion: Converts gradient to kg A⁻¹ and substitutes into $B = (\mathrm{grad}\cdot g)/L$.
Flux density $B = 84.0 mT$.
Substitutes into $F = B I L$.
Magnetic force $F = 0.0136 N$.
Converts $F/g$ into grams.
Mass change $\Delta m = 1.39 g$.
States magnetic field exerts an upward force on the clamped wire.
Applies Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite downward force on magnet yoke raises balance reading.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the power dissipated in the external load I²R, omitting heating I²r inside the rod.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses ε²/R and neglects the rod resistance r when finding loop current.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates magnetic braking force BIL without multiplying by speed v.

items.stem: In the two-stage pulse-shaping circuit shown, a capacitor of capacitance C = 250 μF is first fully charged to V₀ = 9.00 V by closing Switch A while Switches B and C remain open. Switch A is then opened and Switch B is closed so the capacitor discharges through R₁ = 60 kΩ for 10.0 s. At t = 10.0 s, while Switch B stays closed, Switch C is closed to connect R₂ = 30 kΩ in parallel with R₁ for a further 6.00 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b)(i) τ₁ = R₁C = 15.00 s, so V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁) = 4.621 V ≈ 4.62 V (confirming 4.6 V). (b)(ii) R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 20.0 kΩ, giving τ₂ = R_eq C = 5.000 s ≈ 5.00 s. (b)(iii) V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂) = 1.392 V ≈ 1.39 V. (b)(iv) larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

markScheme.criterion: Mentions charge stored per unit potential difference (coulombs per volt).
Complete SI unit definition: capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Evaluates stage-1 time constant τ₁ = R₁C = 15.0 s.
Correctly substitutes V₀, t₁, and τ₁ into V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁).
Shows V₁ = 4.621 V (≥3 s.f.: 4.62 V), clearly matching 4.6 V.
Combines R₁ || R₂ = 20.0 kΩ and calculates τ₂ = R_eq C = 5.00 s.
Substitutes V₁ (accepting rounded prompt value on ECF), t₂, and τ₂ into V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂).
Correct final potential difference V₂ = 1.39 V.
States correctly that V₂ would be larger (smaller/larger matching direction).
Explains via time constants in both stages: larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

parts.prompt: Define the farad.
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the unit definition linking electric charge in coulombs and potential difference in volts.

parts.prompt: Show clearly that after discharging through R₁ alone for 10.0 s, the potential difference across the capacitor is approximately 4.6 V.
parts.expectedAnswer: 4.621 V (which rounds to 4.62 V and 4.6 V)
workingSteps: Stage 1 time constant τ₁ = R₁ C = (60 × 10³ Ω) × (250 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 15.00 s.
Substitute into V₁ = V₀ exp(−t₁ / τ₁) = 9.000 V × exp(−10 / 15.00 s).
Evaluate to 4 s.f.: V₁ = 4.621 V ≈ 4.62 V (confirming approximately 4.6 V).

parts.prompt: At the instant Switch C closes, calculate the new time constant τ₂ of the discharge circuit.
workingSteps: Combined parallel resistance R_eq = (R₁ R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (60 × 30) / (60 + 30) = 20.0 kΩ.
New time constant τ₂ = R_eq C = (20 × 10³ Ω) × (250 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 5.000 s ≈ 5.00 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference V₂ across the capacitor after a further 6.00 s with both Switch B and Switch C closed.
workingSteps: Start Stage 2 decay from V₁ = 4.621 V with time constant τ₂ = 5.000 s.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how the final potential difference V₂ would change if resistor R₁ were replaced by a larger resistor throughout the entire experiment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing the first resistor with a larger resistor gives a larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.
workingSteps: A larger resistance changes both the initial discharge time constant and the combined parallel resistance in the same direction.
Link the altered time constants in both stages to the rate of exponential decay and the remaining potential difference.

items.stem: In a telemetry energy-transfer buffer, capacitor C₁ = 25 μF is charged to V₁ = 41 V, isolated from its supply, and then connected via switch S in parallel with capacitor C₂ = 75 μF (initially uncharged). What final common potential difference is established across both capacitors?
items.workedSolution: Total conserved charge Q_net = C₁V₁ + C₂V₂ = 1.02 × 10⁻³ C. Final parallel capacitance C_eq = 100 μF, so V_f = Q_net / (C₁ + C₂) = 10.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves net charge Q_net and divides by C₁ + C₂ to obtain 10.3 V (C).

items.stem: A fine-beam tube containing low-pressure helium gas accelerates thermionic electrons across 280 V into a uniform magnetic field of 1.50 mT, producing a luminous circular ring of radius 3.76 cm.
items.workedSolution: (a) heating the metal filament gives conduction electrons enough thermal kinetic energy to escape the surface. (b) $e/m = 2V/(B^2 r^2) = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹$. (c) $v = 9.93 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: States current heats the cathode filament.
Explains electrons gain sufficient thermal KE to overcome the work function and escape.
Equates $Bev = mv^2/r$ and $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV$ to eliminate $v$.
Substitutes $V = 280\text{ V}$, $B = 1.50 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$, $r = 0.0376\text{ m}$.
Correct specific charge 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.
Uses $v = \sqrt{2(e/m)V}$ or $v = (e/m)Br$.
Correct electron speed 9.93 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: To locate a patient cross-section $0.120\text{ m}$ from the bore centre, gradient coils add a uniform magnetic-field gradient of $0.0250\text{ T m}^{-1}$. Using $f = (42.6\text{ MHz T}^{-1}) B$, calculate the frequency shift $\Delta f$ of protons in that slice relative to the centre.
items.workedSolution: Field offset $\Delta B = G x = 0.0250 \times 0.120 = 3.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$. Frequency shift $\Delta f = 42.6 \times 10^3\text{ kHz T}^{-1} \times 3.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T} = 128 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 128 kHz.

items.stem: A non-destructive eddy-current probe winding has 200 turns, cross-sectional area 0.008 m², and total loop resistance 5 Ω. Uniform magnetic field lines make an angle of 60° with the plane of the coil while the flux density ramps uniformly from 0.22 T to 0.55 T over 0.025 s. What is the initial magnetic flux linkage NΦ₁ of the coil?
items.workedSolution: Angle to coil normal θ_n = 30°. Initial flux linkage NΦ₁ = NBA cos θ_n = 200 × 0.22 × 0.008 × cos 30° = 0.305 Wb.

markScheme.criterion: Uses θ_normal = 30° in NΦ₁ = NBA cos θ_normal to obtain 0.305 Wb (C).

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed at which the particle enters the magnetic field.
Determine the radius r of the circular trajectory.
Calculate the semicircular strike diameter D = 2r across an exit detector plane.

items.stem: An experimental capacitive MEMS accelerometer features plates of area 0.7 m² at initial spacing 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m filled with a medium of relative permittivity 6.5 and charged to 420 V (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹). The plates are disconnected from the DC source so the plates remain electrically isolated, and the plate separation is then adjusted to 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m while εᵣ stays at 6.5.

markScheme.criterion: Finds initial C = εᵣε₀A/d and applies U_i = ½CV².
Obtains 5.92 × 10⁻³ J.
Evaluates C′ = εᵣε₀A / d′ at the new separation.
Obtains 1.34 × 10⁻⁷ F.
Uses constant charge U_f = Q²/(2C′) and subtracts U_i.
Obtains −2.96 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: High-energy particle physics facilities begin acceleration with a radio-frequency linear accelerator (linac) before injecting beams into detectors or synchrotrons.
items.workedSolution: Alternating radio-frequency fields accelerate particles across drift-tube gaps while curved magnetic tracks reveal charge sign and momentum via r = p over Bq. Adjacent hollow metal drift tubes connect to opposite terminals of a fixed-frequency RF AC supply. Protons accelerate across each gap when the field points forward and travel at constant speed inside each tube (E = 0 inside a conductor) while polarity reverses over half a period T/2 = 1/(2f). At non-relativistic speeds E_k = neV gives v_n ∝ √n so L_n = v_n/(2f) ∝ √n. Near c, kinetic energy rises via relativistic mass-energy while speed approaches c asymptotically, so drift tubes approach a constant maximum length c/(2f).

markScheme.criterion: L1: States adjacent hollow metal drift tubes connect alternately to a fixed-frequency RF AC supply.
L1: Explains electric field is zero inside each conducting tube so protons coast at constant speed inside and accelerate across gaps.
L2: Explains polarity reverses every half-period T/2 = 1/(2f) so the field always accelerates protons forward at each gap.
L2: Combines ½mv² = neV and L_n = v_n/(2f) to deduce non-relativistic tube lengths grow as L_n ∝ √n.
L3: Notes that as proton speeds approach c, relativistic effects limit speed below c despite increasing energy/momentum.
L3: Concludes that at ultra-relativistic speeds drift-tube length approaches a constant value c/(2f).

parts.prompt: Explain how a radio-frequency linac accelerates a beam of protons using alternating drift tubes, why the tubes lengthen as √n at non-relativistic speeds, and how the tube spacing changes once protons approach the speed of light c. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Alternating radio-frequency fields accelerate particles across drift-tube gaps while curved magnetic tracks reveal charge sign and momentum via r = p over Bq. Adjacent hollow metal drift tubes connect to opposite terminals of a fixed-frequency RF AC supply. Protons accelerate across each gap when the field points forward and travel at constant speed inside each tube (E = 0 inside a conductor) while polarity reverses over half a period T/2 = 1/(2f). At non-relativistic speeds E_k = neV gives v_n ∝ √n so L_n = v_n/(2f) ∝ √n. Near c, kinetic energy rises via relativistic mass-energy while speed approaches c asymptotically, so drift tubes approach a constant maximum length c/(2f).
workingSteps: Explain alternating RF connection across adjacent tubes and gap-only acceleration with E = 0 inside tubes.
Link constant drift time T/2 = 1/(2f) with v_n = √(2neV/m) to show L_n ∝ √n.
Explain relativistic saturation: v → c so tube length approaches constant c/(2f).

workingSteps: Parallel branch: C_p = C₂ + C₃ = 100 + 60 = 160 μF.
Series combination: C_eq = (C₁ C_p) / (C₁ + C_p) = (80 × 160) / (80 + 160) = 53.33 μF ≈ 53.3 μF.

parts.expectedAnswer: 75.0 V (limited by the single series capacitor)
workingSteps: In series both sections hold equal charge Q, so V ∝ 1/C; the smaller capacitance (single series capacitor) reaches 50 V first.
Maximum safe total pd V_AB,max = 50 × (1 + 80 / 160) = 75.00 V ≈ 75.0 V.

options.text: With time-base OFF the AC sinusoid forms a crisp vertical line of length V_pp along the central scale; this works because a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

options.label: B
options.text: Switching time-base OFF converts the AC waveform into a single stationary dot whose height equals V_rms.
options.distractorRationale: An AC signal with time-base OFF produces a vertical line of height V_pp, not a stationary dot.

options.label: C
options.text: Switching time-base OFF doubles the magnetic flux linkage through the search coil.
options.distractorRationale: CRO controls affect only display deflection, never the magnetic field or flux linkage.

options.label: D
options.text: Time-base OFF allows the search coil to measure static DC fields accurately.
options.distractorRationale: Static DC fields still produce zero induced emf in a stationary search coil.

items.stem: When switch S closes in an industrial watchdog reset timer, a 25 μF uncharged capacitor charges from a 9 V cell through a 10 kΩ resistor over an interval of 0.375 s. How much electrostatic energy is stored in the capacitor at t = 0.375 s?
items.workedSolution: τ = RC = 0.250 s, giving V_C(0.375 s) = 6.99 V. Stored energy U = ½CV_C² = 0.5 × 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ × (6.99)² = 6.11 × 10⁻⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V_C(t) and computes U(t) = ½CV_C(t)² = 6.11 × 10⁻⁴ J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates maximum stored energy ½CV₀² rather than the instantaneous energy at the query time.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of one-half in U(t) = ½CV_C(t)².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scales stored energy linearly with V_C(t)/V₀ instead of quadratically with (V_C(t)/V₀)² in U = ½CV_C².

items.stem: A power station steps 11.0 kV up using Nₚ = 1000 and Nₛ = 12 000 turns before transmitting 26.4 MW of electrical power along transmission cables of total resistance 10.0 Ω. Calculate the thermal power lost in the transmission cables.
items.workedSolution: Vₛ = 11.0 kV × 12 = 1.32 × 10⁵ V. Line current I = P / Vₛ = 200 A. Cable heating P_loss = I²R = 4.00 × 10⁵ W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds cable heating loss 4.00 × 10⁵ W.

items.stem: A strong neodymium bar magnet falls vertically with its south pole leading toward the upper face of a closed coil. Which pole is induced at the upper face of the coil during approach?
items.workedSolution: To oppose approach of the south pole, Lenz's law produces a south pole induced at the top of the coil repelling the approaching south pole. Therefore the correct statement is: A south pole induced at the top of the coil repelling the approaching south pole

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: south pole induced at the top of the coil repelling the approaching south pole.

items.stem: An aircraft auxiliary AC bus resistive test rig uses a coil of negligible internal resistance with 280 turns and area 0.012 m² spinning at 25 Hz in a uniform 0.22 T magnetic field across a 40 Ω resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε₀ = 2πfNBA.
Obtains 116 V.
Uses I_rms = ε₀ / (√2 R).
Obtains 2.05 A.
Applies P_mean = I_rms² R (= ½ ε₀ I₀).
Obtains 169 W.

items.stem: A planetary-probe isotopic magnetic sector filters potassium ions (charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, masses m₁ = 6.47 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and m₂ = 6.81 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) using crossed fields E = 9.60 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B₁ = 0.25 T, then bends them through semicircular arcs onto a detector plate in a chamber field B₂ = 0.6 T (into the page). How far from the entry slit S does the lighter isotope strike the detector wall?
items.workedSolution: v = E / B₁ = 3.84 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ and r₁ = m₁v / (qB₂) = 0.259 m. Strike distance from slit S is D₁ = 2r₁ = 0.518 m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes D₁ = 2r₁ = 2m₁E / (qB₁B₂) = 0.518 m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports the orbital radius r₁ rather than the semicircular chord distance D₁ = 2r₁ from slit S.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses B₁² instead of B₁B₂ in D₁ = 2m₁E/(qB₁B₂).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the separation ΔD between the two isotopes rather than the slit-to-impact distance 2r₁.

options.distractorRationale: M = M₀ + (BL/g)I remains strictly linear.

options.distractorRationale: The clamped rod is supported by the retort stand, so the intercept is solely the yoke and slab magnets.

Obtains 4.93 C.

items.stem: In the dual-rate relay delay circuit shown, a capacitor of capacitance C = 600 μF is first fully charged to V₀ = 14.0 V by closing Switch A while Switches B and C remain open. Switch A is then opened and Switch B is closed so the capacitor discharges through R₁ = 30 kΩ for 12.0 s. At t = 12.0 s, while Switch B stays closed, Switch C is closed to connect R₂ = 15 kΩ in parallel with R₁ for a further 5.00 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b)(i) τ₁ = R₁C = 18.00 s, so V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁) = 7.188 V ≈ 7.19 V (confirming 7.2 V). (b)(ii) R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 10.0 kΩ, giving τ₂ = R_eq C = 6.000 s ≈ 6.00 s. (b)(iii) V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂) = 3.124 V ≈ 3.12 V. (b)(iv) larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

markScheme.criterion: Mentions charge stored per unit potential difference (coulombs per volt).
Complete SI unit definition: capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Evaluates stage-1 time constant τ₁ = R₁C = 18.0 s.
Correctly substitutes V₀, t₁, and τ₁ into V₁ = V₀ e^(−t₁/τ₁).
Shows V₁ = 7.188 V (≥3 s.f.: 7.19 V), clearly matching 7.2 V.
Combines R₁ || R₂ = 10.0 kΩ and calculates τ₂ = R_eq C = 6.00 s.
Substitutes V₁ (accepting rounded prompt value on ECF), t₂, and τ₂ into V₂ = V₁ e^(−t₂/τ₂).
Correct final potential difference V₂ = 3.12 V.
States correctly that V₂ would be larger (smaller/larger matching direction).
Explains via time constants in both stages: larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.

parts.prompt: Define the farad.
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the unit definition linking electric charge in coulombs and potential difference in volts.

parts.prompt: Show clearly that after discharging through R₁ alone for 12.0 s, the potential difference across the capacitor is approximately 7.2 V.
parts.expectedAnswer: 7.188 V (which rounds to 7.19 V and 7.2 V)
workingSteps: Stage 1 time constant τ₁ = R₁ C = (30 × 10³ Ω) × (600 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 18.00 s.
Substitute into V₁ = V₀ exp(−t₁ / τ₁) = 14.00 V × exp(−12 / 18.00 s).
Evaluate to 4 s.f.: V₁ = 7.188 V ≈ 7.19 V (confirming approximately 7.2 V).

parts.prompt: At the instant Switch C closes, calculate the new time constant τ₂ of the discharge circuit.
workingSteps: Combined parallel resistance R_eq = (R₁ R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (30 × 15) / (30 + 15) = 10.0 kΩ.
New time constant τ₂ = R_eq C = (10 × 10³ Ω) × (600 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 6.000 s ≈ 6.00 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference V₂ across the capacitor after a further 5.00 s with both Switch B and Switch C closed.
workingSteps: Start Stage 2 decay from V₁ = 7.188 V with time constant τ₂ = 6.000 s.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how the final potential difference V₂ would change if resistor R₁ were replaced by a larger resistor throughout the entire experiment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing the first resistor with a larger resistor gives a larger final potential difference because the time constant increases and the capacitor discharges more slowly.
workingSteps: A larger resistance changes both the initial discharge time constant and the combined parallel resistance in the same direction.
Link the altered time constants in both stages to the rate of exponential decay and the remaining potential difference.

items.stem: On a switched-capacitor sample-and-hold stage, an isolated capacitor C₁ of capacitance 30 μF at V₁ = 23 V is bridged across a second capacitor C₂ of capacitance 50 μF that is charged separately to V₂ = 7 V and connected with like polarity.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Q_net = C₁V₁ + C₂V₂ before switch closure.
Obtains 1.04 × 10⁻³ C.
Divides conserved charge from (a) by C₁ + C₂.
Obtains 13.0 V.
Subtracts final stored energy ½(C₁ + C₂)V_f² from initial stored energy.
Obtains 2.40 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: A clinical $1.50\text{ T}$ MR scanner applies a field gradient of $0.0200\text{ T m}^{-1}$ along the patient axis to isolate a $5.00\text{ mm}$ thick cross-section. The proton precession frequency is $f = (42.6\text{ MHz T}^{-1}) B$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_0 = 42.6 \times 1.50 = 63.9 MHz$. (b) $\Delta B = 0.0200 \times 5.00 \times 10^{-3} = 1.00 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}$, giving $\Delta f = 4.26 kHz$. (c) gradient field coils vary magnetic flux density across the patient to scan successive small regions.

markScheme.criterion: Correct frequency 63.9 MHz.
Calculates $\Delta B = 0.0200 \times 5.00 \times 10^{-3} = 1.00 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}$.
Correct slice bandwidth 4.26 kHz.
Explains gradient field coils vary magnetic flux density across the patient to scan successive small regions.
Notes unique local $B$ gives a unique resonant RF frequency for spatial mapping.

items.stem: During a dielectric bench test, a silicone elastomer sheet with relative permittivity 3.2 completely fills the 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m gap between parallel metal plates of area 1.5 m² inside an industrial proximity-sensing pad. When the assembly is charged to 320 V (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹), calculate the energy stored per unit volume inside the dielectric.
items.workedSolution: Uniform field E = V / d = 320 / 0.0003 = 1.07 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. Energy density u_E = ½εᵣε₀E² = 0.5 × 3.2 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × (1.07 × 10⁶)² = 16.1 J m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = V/d and u_E = ½εᵣε₀E² to obtain 16.1 J m⁻³ (B).

Obtains 0.248 Wb.
Applies Faraday's law |ε| = |NΦ₂ − NΦ₁| / Δt.
Obtains 14.9 V.
Divides induced emf from (b) by coil resistance R.
Obtains 0.930 A.

items.stem: During calibration of an electrostatic-gun magnetic spectrometer, initially stationary singly ionised lithium ions (charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 1.16 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) are accelerated by 1800 V and directed normal to a 0.250 T field (out of the page). What speed does the particle reach upon entering the magnetic field?
items.workedSolution: Equating ½mv² = |q|V_acc gives v = √(2|q|V_acc / m) = √(2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1800 / 1.16 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) = 2.23 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = √(2|q|V_acc / m) = 2.23 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: An experimental capacitive MEMS accelerometer features plates of area 0.7 m² at initial spacing 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ m filled with a medium of relative permittivity 6.5 and charged to 420 V (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹). The plates are disconnected from the DC source so the plates remain electrically isolated, and the plate separation is then adjusted to 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m while εᵣ stays at 6.5. What is the new potential difference across the isolated plates?
items.workedSolution: For isolated plates, charge Q is conserved while C′ = C₀(d/d′). Therefore V′ = Q / C′ = V₀(d′/d) = 420 × (0.0003 / 0.0006) = 210 V.

markScheme.criterion: Uses charge conservation V′ = V₀(d′/d) to obtain 210 V (B).

items.stem: During testing of a camera strobe flash bank, an engineer connects uncharged capacitors C₁ = 12 μF and C₂ = 24 μF in series with a steady 43 V cell.

markScheme.criterion: Applies reciprocal series rule 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
Obtains 8.00 × 10⁻⁶ F.
Uses Q = C_eq V₀ and V₁ = Q / C₁.
Obtains 28.7 V.
Applies U = ½C_eq V₀².
Obtains 7.40 × 10⁻³ J.

items.stem: Injected orthogonally at 2.20 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ into the 0.220 T magnetic field (directed into the page) of a bubble-chamber momentum analyser, an alpha particle (q = +3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) undergoes uniform circular motion in vacuum. What is the cyclotron revolution frequency f of the particle in this magnetic field?

markScheme.criterion: Applies f = |q|B / (2πm) = 1.69 × 10⁶ Hz (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the formula and evaluates orbital period 2πm / (|q|B) instead of frequency.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes angular speed ω = |q|B / m and omits dividing by 2π for frequency f = ω / (2π).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides ω by π instead of 2π when converting angular speed to frequency.

items.stem: A bubble-chamber photograph shows two symmetric spirals emerging suddenly from an empty point in the liquid and curving in opposite directions. Which physical interpretation explains this signature?
items.workedSolution: An invisible neutral photon undergoes pair production γ → e⁻ + e⁺; equal-magnitude opposite charges curve oppositely with matched initial radii. Therefore the correct statement is: An uncharged gamma photon leaves no track before creating an electron and positron of opposite charge that curve in opposite directions with identical initial radii.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: an uncharged gamma photon leaves no track before creating an electron and positron of opposite charge that curve in opposite directions with identical initial radii.

options.label: A
options.text: An uncharged gamma photon leaves no track before creating an electron and positron of opposite charge that curve in opposite directions with identical initial radii.

options.label: B
options.text: A single negatively charged proton splits spontaneously into two neutrons that curve apart in the magnetic field.
options.distractorRationale: Protons are positive, neutrons are uncharged and leave no curved tracks, and charge conservation would fail.

options.label: C
options.text: An incoming gamma photon leaves a thick straight ionisation track before bouncing off an electron at rest.
options.distractorRationale: Uncharged photons cannot directly ionise along a continuous track and therefore leave no visible trail before the vertex.

options.label: D
options.text: Two electrons enter from opposite ends of the chamber and annihilate at the vertex to produce a stationary proton.
options.distractorRationale: Two identical charges moving in the same direction curve the same way, and two electrons cannot annihilate into a proton.

items.stem: Within a vacuum accelerator monochromatic ion collimator, a proton (+1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is injected horizontally to the right at 1.50 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ between plates 0.015 m apart at p.d. 750 V (upper plate negative) inside a perpendicular 0.2 T field (out of the page). What is the initial upward transverse acceleration of the proton upon entering the crossed fields?
items.workedSolution: E = V/d = 5.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Upward electric force F_E = qE = 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁵ N; downward magnetic force |F_B| = qvB = 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. Net upward acceleration a_y = (F_E − |F_B|) / m = 1.92 × 10¹² m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing qvB from qE and divides by m to obtain 1.92 × 10¹² m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: In the audio crossover filter shown between terminals A and B, capacitor C₁ = 40 μF is connected in series with the parallel pair C₂ = 70 μF and C₃ = 50 μF. Every capacitor has a maximum safe working voltage of 60 V. What is the maximum safe potential difference that can be applied across terminals A and B without exceeding the rating of any capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel pair C_p = C₂ + C₃ = 120 μF. Because C₁ (40 μF) and C_p (120 μF) carry equal series charge Q, the smaller capacitance (single series capacitor) reaches 60 V first. Thus V_AB,max = 60 × (1 + 40 / 120) = 80.00 V ≈ 80.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the single series capacitor limits the voltage and calculates V_AB,max = 80.0 V.

items.stem: In Required Practical 11, a search coil with $N = 1500$ turns of area 2.0 cm² is centred inside a large circular coil driven by a 60 Hz AC supply. With the CRO Y-gain set to 100 mV div⁻¹ and the coil normal at $\theta = 48^\circ$ to the field, the peak-to-peak vertical trace spans 4.84 divisions.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 484 mV$. (b) Gradient $= 724 mV$. (c) $B = 3.20 mT$. (d) a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies peak-to-peak divisions by Y-gain.
$V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 484 mV$.
Divides $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ by $\cos 48^\circ$.
Gradient $= 724 mV$.
Applies $V_{\mathrm{pp,max}} = 4\pi f B A N$ with $A$ in m².
Peak flux density $B = 3.20 mT$.
Static DC field gives zero rate of change of flux linkage, so zero induced emf.
Use a Hall probe to measure static DC magnetic flux density.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak-to-peak induced voltage $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ at $\theta = 48^\circ$.
Hence calculate the gradient of the straight-line graph of $V_{\mathrm{pp}}$ against $\cos\theta$.
Use $\varepsilon_0 = 2\pi f B A N$ to determine the peak magnetic flux density $B$ in mT.
workingSteps: Gradient $= 4\pi f B A N$, so $B = (724\times 10^{-3}) / (4\pi \times 60 \times 2\times 10^{-4} \times 1500) = 3.20 mT$.

parts.prompt: Explain why the search coil fails if the AC supply is replaced by a DC battery, and state what sensor should be used instead.
parts.expectedAnswer: a search coil requires an alternating magnetic field to induce an emf whereas a hall probe measures static direct current magnetic flux density
workingSteps: Faraday's law requires rate of change of flux linkage d(NΦ)/dt ≠ 0, which is zero in static DC.
Use a calibrated Hall probe (perpendicular to field) for static DC flux density.

Obtains 0.400 s.

Obtains 4.02 V.
Uses U = ½CV_C² with the voltage found in (b).
Obtains 6.47 × 10⁻⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the RC time constant τ of the circuit.
Determine the potential difference across the capacitor at t = 0.16 s.
Calculate the electrostatic energy stored in the capacitor at t = 0.16 s.

items.stem: An armature of 400 turns and area 0.018 m² in a hydroelectric micro-turbine alternator spins at frequency 20 Hz within a uniform 0.35 T field; its coil normal is aligned with the field at t = 0, and an oscilloscope reads the output at t = 0.00833 s. What instantaneous emf ε is induced at t = 0.00833 s?
items.workedSolution: ω = 2π(20) = 126 rad s⁻¹, ε₀ = NBAω = 317 V. At t = 0.00833 s, ε(t) = ε₀ sin(ωt) = 274 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes ε₀ = 2πfNBA and evaluates ε₀ sin(ωt) = 274 V (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports the maximum amplitude ε₀ rather than evaluating ε(t) = ε₀ sin(ωt) at the specified instant.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits 2π when computing peak amplitude NBAω before multiplying by sin(ωt).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ε₀ cos(ωt) instead of ε₀ sin(ωt), confusing the phase of induced emf with magnetic flux linkage.

items.stem: Inside the vacuum chamber of an inkjet micro-droplet deflection stage, electrodes 0.04 m long and 0.05 m apart are biased at 1820 V while an electron (q = −1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) enters centrally at 1.60 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the transverse deflection as the particle exits the plates?
items.workedSolution: Transit time t = L / v₀ = 0.04 / 1.60 × 10⁷ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁹ s. Transverse acceleration a_y = |q|V / (md) = 6.39 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻². Deflection |Δy| = ½ a_y t² = 0.0200 m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates t = L/v₀, a_y = |q|V/(md), and |Δy| = ½a_y t² = 0.0200 m (B).

items.stem: The diagram shows a proton cyclotron with two hollow metal D-shaped electrodes (dees) in a uniform perpendicular magnetic field. What are the distinct roles of the magnetic field and the electric field?
items.workedSolution: Inside the shielded metal dees, B provides centripetal force without changing speed; across the gap, the alternating electric field does work qV. Therefore the correct statement is: During acceleration, ions follow semicircular paths inside hollow metal D-shaped dees under a perpendicular magnetic field and are accelerated across the gap by an alternating electric field that reverses every half-period.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: ions follow semicircular paths inside hollow metal D-shaped dees under a perpendicular magnetic field and are accelerated across the gap by an alternating electric field that reverses every half-period.

options.label: A
options.text: The uniform magnetic field does work on the protons inside the dees to increase their speed while the electric field bends them into semicircles.
options.distractorRationale: Magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity and does zero work; only the electric field across the gap increases kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.text: A steady direct voltage between the dees accelerates the protons continuously around every circular turn inside the hollow metal.
options.distractorRationale: Inside a hollow metal conductor E = 0, and a steady DC voltage would decelerate ions on every alternate crossing.

options.label: C
options.text: During acceleration, ions follow semicircular paths inside hollow metal D-shaped dees under a perpendicular magnetic field and are accelerated across the gap by an alternating electric field that reverses every half-period.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnetic field reverses direction every half-turn so that ions spiral outward at constant radius.
options.distractorRationale: The magnetic field stays constant while the electric p.d. across the gap alternates; radius grows with speed.

items.stem: To verify the peak amplitude of a noisy mains-frequency signal without triggering jitter, a technician turns the oscilloscope time-base knob to OFF. How should peak voltage V₀ be obtained from the resulting display?
items.workedSolution: Switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage, so V₀ = V_pp / 2. Therefore the correct statement is: Measure half the vertical trace height because switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Measure the full length of the vertical trace directly because the trace runs only from zero to +V₀.
options.distractorRationale: AC swings symmetrically from −V₀ to +V₀, so total length is V_pp = 2V₀.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure the distance of the stationary dot from the centre horizontal graticule line.
options.distractorRationale: Only a steady DC signal gives a stationary dot with time-base OFF.

options.label: C
options.text: Divide the full vertical trace length by root two to obtain peak voltage V₀ directly.
options.distractorRationale: V_pp / √2 equals 2 V_rms, neither V₀ nor V_rms.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure half the vertical trace height because switching off the time base collapses an alternating sinusoid into a vertical central line of length equal to the peak-to-peak voltage

items.stem: A small cylindrical magnet dropped down a long vertical non-magnetic copper pipe falls far more slowly than an identical unmagnetised brass cylinder (where g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What physics explains this dramatic braking?
items.workedSolution: Falling flux induces eddy currents in the copper tube: induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy. Therefore the correct statement is: Eddy currents arise in the copper wall because induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it so mechanical work done against magnetic opposition converts into electrical thermal energy obeying conservation of energy.

items.stem: Across a pure 40 Ω load in a standby hospital alternator feeding a resistive heater, a coil of 280 turns and area 0.012 m² (negligible coil resistance) rotates uniformly at 40 Hz inside a 0.38 T magnetic field. What mean electrical power is dissipated in the resistive load over a complete cycle?
items.workedSolution: Peak emf ε₀ = 2πfNBA = 321 V; V_rms = ε₀ / √2 = 227 V. Mean resistive power P_mean = V_rms² / R = ½ ε₀² / R = 1.29 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Computes ε₀ = 2πfNBA and mean power P_mean = ½ε₀²/R = 1.29 × 10³ W (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides V₀ by 2 instead of √2 before squaring in V_rms²/R, introducing a ¼ factor.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates peak instantaneous power V₀²/R without applying the ½ sinusoidal average factor.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides peak power V₀I₀ by √2 instead of 2, forgetting that both V_rms = V₀/√2 and I_rms = I₀/√2 contribute a 1/√2 factor.

items.stem: In Required Practical 10, a stiff copper wire of active length $L = 60$ mm sits perpendicularly between slab magnets mounted on a steel yoke atop a 0.01 g digital top-pan balance ($g = 9.81$ m s⁻²). Plotting balance reading against current $I$ up to 4.5 A produces a straight line of gradient 0.330 g A⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $B = 54.0 mT$. (b) $F = 0.0146 N$. (c) $\Delta m = 1.49 g$. (d) by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current.

markScheme.criterion: Converts gradient to kg A⁻¹ and substitutes into $B = (\mathrm{grad}\cdot g)/L$.
Flux density $B = 54.0 mT$.
Substitutes into $F = B I L$.
Magnetic force $F = 0.0146 N$.
Converts $F/g$ into grams.
Mass change $\Delta m = 1.49 g$.
States magnetic field exerts an upward force on the clamped wire.
Applies Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite downward force on magnet yoke raises balance reading.

parts.prompt: Use the gradient to calculate the magnetic flux density $B$ in mT.
Calculate the magnetic force on the wire at the maximum current of 4.5 A.
Calculate the change in balance reading $\Delta m$ (in g) at this maximum current.
Explain using Newton's third law why the balance reading changes even though the wire is clamped independently.
parts.expectedAnswer: by newton third law the equal and opposite downward magnetic force on the magnet yoke increases the top pan balance reading proportionally to current
workingSteps: Magnetic field exerts an upward force BIl on the current-carrying wire.
By Newton's 3rd law, the wire exerts an equal downward force BIl on the magnets/yoke, increasing the balance normal reaction.

items.stem: Connected to a charge integrator of total loop resistance 2 Ω, a flat earth-inductor compass loop containing 140 turns of area 0.022 m² faces normal to a field that reverses from +0.12 T to −0.120 T in 0.2 s. What total magnitude of electric charge ΔQ flows around the circuit during this reversal?
items.workedSolution: Signed field change |ΔB| = |-0.12 − 0.12| = 0.24 T, so |Δ(NΦ)| = 140 × 0.24 × 0.022 = 0.739 Wb. Induced charge ΔQ = |Δ(NΦ)| / R = 0.370 C.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for field sign reversal in |Δ(NΦ)| and evaluates ΔQ = |Δ(NΦ)|/R = 0.370 C (A).

items.stem: A uniform 0.6 T magnetic field directed out of the page permeates a linear regenerator test track whose smooth conducting rails sit 0.32 m apart across a 2.4 Ω external resistor. An external agent pulls a rod of resistance 0.6 Ω to the right at constant speed 8 m s⁻¹. What is the terminal potential difference across the external load resistor?
items.workedSolution: ε = BLv = 1.54 V; loop current I = ε / (R + r) = 0.512 A. Terminal p.d. across load V_term = I R = 0.512 × 2.4 = 1.23 V.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_term = BLv × R/(R + r) to obtain 1.23 V (A).
